cards.answer: I decide what failure costs before I compare, then let that criterion pick. At UIC the institutional use was finding students likely to discontinue, so error on that class decided it: H2O's random forest kept error below 5% across all three classes in cross-validation, while CatBoost's error on the Discontinued class was 47.71% with a systematic residual. For legislative extraction, the job was 11,673 bills and roughly 155 unattended hours, so I weighted stability over peak: Mistral at 500 tokens swung 0.10 in rubric score across chunk sizes against 0.35 for Qwen, even though Qwen had the higher single score. And I re-run the comparison when conditions change. After the vLLM migration, production moved to Llama 3.1 8B because the recovered headroom made the larger model affordable.

cards.answer: The clearest example: an archival image job on a single NVIDIA L4 was going to take 22 hours, with the GPU only 28% busy. I ran a controlled benchmark that held the model and hardware fixed and varied the serving stack and concurrency, and found the bottleneck was request serialization in Ollama, not the GPU or the model. Moving to vLLM's continuous batching gave a 6.22x speedup at concurrency 8 on the same card: 22 hours down to 3.7, GPU use up to 97%. I then ran a multi-model sweep on vLLM for the legislative pipeline (chunk size, concurrency, telemetry, SLO gate) to pick and size the production model. Both studies are in my Applied AI Lab.

cards.answer: I size from measured throughput at the real load, not the spec sheet. Quality stayed within 0.6 points from concurrency 1 to 24, so the recommendation was concurrency 12 to 24. For document intelligence I sized every model for a single L4 (24 GB) or L40S (48 GB), one model on the card at a time, and measured all of them on the same 32 GB desktop so speeds compare fairly.

cards.answer: First, I find candidates that fit the hardware at the context, output length and concurrency we need, and I check each licence, with the current model as the baseline. Second, I turn the real task into a frozen test with code-based checks, keeping failures and timeouts in the denominator. Third, I write the decision rule before the run: the primary measure, the minimum useful improvement, and what a pass earns. Then I check that the harness reproduces the baseline, change one thing at a time, and confirm any winner on fresh cases. Size and benchmark scores are only a starting point: a smaller model beat a bigger one in two of my evaluations.

cards.answer: No. In my document evaluation, the 0.9B PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 beat Qwen3-VL 32B on financial tables, 0.852 vs 0.762 TEDS. In my generation screen, Qwen3.8 27B accepted 7 of 20 groups against 3 for the larger Qwen3-32B, and held up on 60 new groups. Size sets capacity. It doesn't tell you how well a model was trained or how well it fits your task. Training recipe, quantization, server and chat template all change behaviour: the same 32B accepted 3 groups under one backend and 1 under another. A model that fits fully on the card also runs faster, which matters when a pipeline retries.

In my generation screen, Gemma 4 had the highest IFEval score of the four models completed, 0.900, and accepted 0 of 20 task groups. Qwen3.8 had the lowest IFEval score, 0.806, and accepted the most. cards.answer: Route each task to the cheapest model that meets its quality bar, measured on our own hardware. Cache LLM responses by prompt hash, so repeated queries cost nothing. cards.title: Reading a model's name: 27B, 35B-A3B, Q4_K_M, AWQ
questions: what does q4_k_m mean
what does the q4_k_m at the end of a model name actually mean
35b-a3b meaning
what does 35b-a3b mean
what does awq mean
what do the numbers in a model name mean
is a 32b model better than a 27b
what does 8b mean in a model name
how to read a model name
what is a mixture of experts model
q4 quantization meaning
cards.answer: The labels look like a ranking and aren't one. 27B or 32B is roughly the parameter count in billions: it sets capacity, not how well the model was trained or follows instructions. 35B-A3B is a mixture of experts: about 35 billion parameters in total with about 3 billion active per token, so it can compute less per token, but all the weights still have to be stored. Q4 or Q4_K_M is an approximately 4-bit weight quantization format, which shrinks the weights so a large model fits on one card. AWQ is a quantization method, not a bit width, so check the actual bit width of the checkpoint you download. My guide walks through each label and what it does and doesn't tell you.

cards.title: Incremental change detection with an anti-join
questions: how do you detect new records when the source has no change feed

anti-join change detection

cards.answer: When a source gives me no change feed, I compute the delta myself and make the delta the work queue. For research proposals, the pipeline queries Kuali for every current proposal and award attachment ID, queries the destination tables for IDs already processed, and anti-joins the two sets in Python. Only net-new document IDs move on to BLOB retrieval. I chose that over a database link because the two Oracle databases sit in different security zones, and a cross-zone dblink is operationally expensive and policy-sensitive. Diffing in Python keeps the boundary intact and lets the pipeline run from anywhere with credentials to both sides. An empty delta is a normal outcome: the stage logs SUCCESS and exits cleanly, so the monitor doesn't mistake a quiet day for a failure. The limit is that an ID anti-join sees new records, not edits; where content changes matter, as with legislation, I compare content hashes instead.

cards.title: Rollback SQL and post-write verification on database writes
questions: what does the auto generated rollback sql look like

cards.answer: I make a write safe to repeat and cheap to undo before I worry about anything else. In the research proposals pipeline every insert into the Oracle staging tables is INSERT WHERE NOT EXISTS or a MERGE, so re-running an already processed batch is a no-op. After each write the pipeline queries the destination database and compares the confirmed row count with the count it attempted; a shortfall raises a RuntimeError inside the run, not in a dashboard a week later. Every run prints its rollback SQL to the log: DELETE statements carrying the exact FILE_DATA_ID list and an UPDATE_TIMESTAMP filter, so recovery doesn't require reading code. The one operation that can't be idempotent, the production TRUNCATE, is double-gated behind dry_run=False and confirm_production=True, both set explicitly. That's a little ceremony per run, and it's cheap next to a half-written table.

cards.title: Point-in-time extraction from the data warehouse
questions: how do you build a historical training set from mutable warehouse tables

cards.answer: If source rows are mutable, I read them as of the date I'm modeling, never as of today. Rebuilding the retirement risk forecast, I built a training panel the original never had: annual point-in-time snapshots from 2005 onward, each anchor capturing exactly who was active that day and labeling them forward twelve months. That came to 4,891 person-year rows across 622 people at a 2.4% base rate. Every anchor uses strict effective-dated reads; current rows read as of today would have corrupted every historical example while looking correct. The last usable anchor sits twelve months before the run date, so a missing retirement is a true negative, not an unfinished window. Splits are by anchor year only. SQL lives in version-controlled files with shared cohort CTEs, and the run aborts if the panel returns fewer than 30 positives. I also logged a defect for the warehouse team: two incompatible service-year definitions.

cards.title: Design: incremental loads from a rate-limited API
questions: how would you design incremental loads from an api with rate limits

cards.answer: I'd let the cheapest possible call decide whether any expensive call happens. On the legislative pipeline that's one LegiScan hash check per run, then downloads only for sessions whose hash changed: 2 to 4 calls on a normal day instead of a full pull. Second, politeness belongs in the client, not in each caller. In my personal Drop Radar project, which polls about 40 sources, each source has its own interval, hosts are spaced, and a 403 or 429 triggers per-host backoff. A bug taught me the third rule: back off by skipping the blocked host, never by sleeping, because a sleeping backoff froze the whole loop for up to an hour. Fourth, persist the hash or cursor only after the data has landed, so a failed run retries rather than skips. On a shared LLM server I also rate-limited calls and gated the full run behind a five-case sanity check.

cards.title: Manifest design: one row per path, pointers and derived fields
questions: walk me through the rims manifest schema

cards.answer: The RIMS manifest is one row per file path, 116 columns, written as partitioned Parquet, and a few choices in it do most of the work. One row per path, never collapsed: a file in three places is three archival facts, so deduplication is recorded in duplicate_of and duplicate_count instead of deleting rows. Per-stage status columns are null until that stage runs, so the queue is a query (WHERE s03_status IS NULL) and 'not reached' differs from 'found nothing'. Extracted text and embeddings live outside as pointers, because 384-dimension vectors at five million rows is about 7.5 GB in a column almost nothing reads. The layer field is recomputed from decision columns, never typed in, so it can't drift. Schema testing caught two bugs I kept as teaching examples: NaN is truthy, which put every row in layer 0, and adding a hundred columns one at a time fragments a DataFrame.

cards.title: File identity, deduplication and quarantine instead of delete
questions: how do you deduplicate files in an archive
blake2b file uid

cards.answer: I separate identity from content, and I record deduplication as a decision rather than a deletion. Each manifest row gets a deterministic file_uid, a blake2b hash over the source identifier plus the normalized path, so re-crawling an accession yields identical keys and successive manifest generations join cleanly. Content duplicates are found by hash, but the rows stay and carry duplicate_of and duplicate_count. The free-filter tier drops NSRL known files, zero-byte files, lock files, .DS_Store and Thumbs.db, caches, node_modules and .git internals before anything expensive runs. Exclusion is written into the manifest, never applied as a removal, so every disposal is auditable and reversible, which is what retention obligations require. The 40 to 70% reduction from that tier is a working estimate in an explicit assumptions table, and I required it to be measured on a complete drive before anyone sizes hardware on it.

cards.answer: My default is to plug proven preservation software into the pipeline rather than write a first-pass layer myself. For the RIMS build I directed a structured evaluation of Siegfried and DROID for PRONOM format identification, BitCurator for write-blocked forensic acquisition and disk imaging, ExifTool, Apache Tika, Docling, the NSRL Reference Data Set, ePADD, Preservica and Archivematica, scored against a rubric. The deliverable was a recommendation: what to adopt, what to skip, and what genuinely remains to be written. The reasoning is maintenance. If professional software sits behind an adapter, its updates arrive for free, and where the university already holds a license we use it. The stage boundary makes that possible: stage 01 takes a root path and walks it, whether it's a mounted drive, an SMB share, a forensic image or a Box folder. Facts in a file header are read, never inferred by a model.

cards.answer: I route every file to an extractor by type and make sure nothing is silently dropped. The legacy file archive covered 15+ types: PyPDF2 for PDFs, python-docx for .docx, BeautifulSoup for HTML, striprtf for RTF, zipfile for archives, a local vision model for images, and column structure for spreadsheets. Corrupted and custom-extension files fell back to filename cleanup, extension inference and folder-level summarization. The weak point was legacy Office: .doc, .xls and .ppt went through Win32 COM automation, which can't run on Colab or the Linux GPU server, can't be parallelized safely, and hangs on malformed files. So for the unified pipeline, porting that path to Apache Tika plus headless LibreOffice is a prerequisite rather than cleanup, with output parity checked against the proof of concept on the same files. Every extraction loop checkpoints per batch and resumes without redoing finished files.

cards.title: Handling bad records without dropping them
questions: what do you do with records that fail to parse

cards.answer: A bad record should become a counted, labeled row, not an exception that kills the batch or a row that quietly disappears. In the research proposals pipeline a four-byte magic-number check catches DOCX files misnamed as .pdf, and they go to a rejection bucket with a reason code. Null BLOBs are counted against the expected total and logged as warnings. Documents with fewer than 40 valid words after cleaning are marked SUCCESSFULLY_PARSED=N and still flow to the output beside the parsed ones. The monitor applies the same rule to itself: an unreadable log becomes a synthetic LOG_READ_FAILED record that can alert. The opposite failure needs a guard too. One malformed bill failed, was never written, reappeared as a delta and failed again for six days; the remedy I specified is a length guard plus a retry ceiling that parks it. That's a dead-letter queue by another name.

cards.title: Email ingestion at scale, and what I'd change

cards.answer: The email archive was a parsing problem first and an AI problem second. A 20-year PST export became 44,677 .eml files with readpst, keeping the folder hierarchy. I walked the tree with os.walk, parsed single-part and multipart MIME with Python's email library, kept text/plain parts with a UTF-8 fallback, and stored the folder path as queryable Folder_N columns. Splitting threads on the Original Message delimiter exploded the files into 79,676 message rows, and regex header extraction gave each From, Sent, To, Cc and Subject. Output was written in batches to CSV, resuming from the existing row count. What I'd change: summarization ran at about 34.78 seconds per email because the Ollama CLI reloaded the model on every call, so 100,000 rows projected to roughly 40 days. I'd serve the model persistently over HTTP and key resume on a row ID hash rather than a row count.

cards.title: The logging contract behind pipeline monitoring
questions: what columns are in your pipeline log schema
explain the logging contract
pipeline_start and pipeline_end sentinel rows

run id shared across stages

cards.answer: Centralized monitoring only works if every pipeline logs the same way, so the log schema is a contract. Each pipeline writes a Parquet log with workflow_name, a run_id shared by every stage of one execution, script_name and script_order, a status (SUCCESS, FAILED, UPSTREAM_FAILED, PIPELINE_START, PIPELINE_END), an is_success flag, UTC event times and durations, and on failure the error type, message, traceback and failure stage. The START and END sentinel rows make silence detectable: a run with a start and no end is incomplete. UPSTREAM_FAILED separates the root cause from the cascade it caused, so one failure doesn't read as five. The retirement pipeline rewrites its log after every event, so a process killed mid-run still records the attempt. Onboarding a new pipeline is one path added to a config list, with no new monitor code.

cards.title: Silence thresholds and alert severity tiers
questions: how do you decide which pipeline failures send an alert

cards.answer: Alerts are tiered by status and age so only actionable failures interrupt anyone. CRITICAL is a FAILED or LOG_READ_FAILED record in the last 24 hours, WARNING is a failure within 7 days, INFO is anything older plus UPSTREAM_FAILED cascade rows. Only CRITICAL sends email, but that email carries the WARNING and INFO rows as context. Silence is detected separately from failure: the monitor computes hours since each pipeline's last successful run and flags any past its threshold. The standard is 48 hours. A quarterly pipeline would breach that two days after every run and then alert for 89 days, so the retirement pipeline has a per-pipeline override of 2,400 hours, with matching Grafana targets. Mail goes through the server's local sendmail, because outbound SMTP isn't available there. The monitor itself runs on cron every 30 to 60 minutes.

cards.title: Auditing the monitor: drift, rosters and unverified alerts
questions: have you audited your own monitoring

cards.answer: A monitor is a pipeline too, so I audit it like one. My July 2026 audit of the legislative pipeline found four things. Stages emitted a success record while producing zero output, so a failing job reported green; the fix I specified makes completion require a non-zero output count. The roster was inferred from whatever happened to log, and the two most broken stages weren't in it; it should be declared. Configuration had drifted: a documented 6 AM schedule for a job that ran at 4 AM, thresholds defined but never imported. And delivery was never verified: the code handed mail to the transport without checking the return value, and sender and recipient domains differed, so a month of 'alerts sent' could have been alerts never delivered. In my Drop Radar personal project, a watcher raises an alarm when no source has been checked for 30 minutes; it fired 34 minutes into a real outage.

cards.title: Scheduling choices: cron, JupyterHub Scheduler and timer Functions, not Airflow
questions: why didn't you use airflow

orchestration trade-offs

cards.answer: I matched each scheduler to where the job runs and put the real investment into knowing whether jobs did their work. The proposals pipeline and the monitor run on cron; the retirement report runs on cron at 06:00 on the first day of each quarter; the daily legislative rescore runs on the JupyterHub Scheduler at 4 AM; weekly digests and nightly impact scoring are timer-triggered Azure Functions. I haven't run Airflow in production. As the one person productionalizing that server, the gap I felt was observability, so I built the alerting and run-tracking layer myself. Dependencies inside a pipeline are explicit stages under one logger, with cascade status, and I decouple jobs that shouldn't share fate: the bill investigator is separate so it can't take down nightly scoring, and heavy jobs moved off JupyterHub after an out-of-memory failure. If cross-pipeline dependencies multiplied, a DAG orchestrator is where I'd go.

cards.title: Batch versus streaming ingestion
questions: batch or streaming ingestion

cards.answer: I pick the cadence from when the data stops being useful. Almost all my institutional work is batch: research proposals run on a schedule where 'nothing new' is a valid outcome, the legislative rescore runs daily, and the retirement report runs quarterly. Bills move over days and that report is read quarterly, so seconds buy nothing. My personal Drop Radar project is the opposite case: limited releases sell out in minutes, so it polls about 40 sources on per-source intervals that tighten inside known drop windows. Its Discord feed moved from 10-second REST polling to the official Gateway over a standard-library websocket with heartbeat, resume and dead-connection detection, so posts arrive in about a second, with polling as automatic fallback. An arrival log records each alert's upstream post, detection and send times. I haven't run Kafka or a managed streaming platform in production.

cards.title: Backfills, catch-up and reprocessing
questions: how do you run a backfill

cards.answer: A backfill should be one command and safe to kill. For the legislative corpus I built a single-command session backfill runner, so each additional General Assembly session is one invocation rather than a hand-staged chain; four full sessions went through every stage with all artifacts verified in Azure. The extractor flushes in batches and can be killed and restarted without double-writing, which an 11,673-bill run of roughly 155 hours requires, and each evaluation configuration wrote to its own isolated path so runs couldn't share state. When extraction silently stopped for 11 nights after a kernel update disabled the GPU driver, I protected the catch-up so no data was skipped. For routine reprocessing, nightly impact scoring keys on a content hash per bill, so only changed bills are re-evaluated, and the passage model trains on nine sessions while the application serves four.

cards.title: Design: ingesting and classifying millions of documents nightly
questions: how would you build a pipeline to ingest and classify millions of documents nightly

cards.answer: I'd build it the way I designed the RIMS archival pipeline: cheap deterministic work first, expensive inference only on what survives. Inventory from metadata before downloading, as our Box ingest does with name, size, SHA-1, path and timestamps. A free-filter tier drops exact duplicates, NSRL known files and junk at zero cost. A manifest with one row per file and per-stage status columns makes each night's work queue a query and every run resumable. Classification runs on the survivors through a batching server: moving to vLLM continuous batching gave 6.22x on the same L4, taking 12,125 images from about 22 hours to 3.7. Writes stay idempotent, every stage logs to the shared contract, and silence alerts. The honest scale note: the unified system has run 2,375 real files in about 21 seconds on 4 vCPU; I haven't run millions nightly, and I'd measure the filter's reduction rate before sizing hardware.

cards.title: Design: making a pipeline restartable after a crash
questions: how would you make a pipeline restartable after a crash mid run

cards.answer: I design so a crash costs at most one batch and a restart needs no human decisions. Three mechanisms do most of it. State lives in the data: in the RIMS manifest a null stage status means not reached, so a restart queries for nulls, and 'processed, found nothing' isn't confused with 'never ran'. Work is flushed in batches and writes are idempotent: the legislative extractor can be killed and restarted without double-writing, and the proposal writes are WHERE NOT EXISTS or MERGE. And the log is rewritten after every event, so a killed process still records that it started. I clear temp directories at the start of each run so stale files can't contaminate the new one, and I cap retries so a poison record gets parked instead of failing forever. My early resumable CSVs resumed from a row count; I'd key resume on record ID hashes now, so a reordered input can't skip or repeat rows.

cards.title: Storage formats: Parquet, CSV or a database
questions: why parquet instead of csv

cards.answer: I choose storage by who reads it and how. Parquet is my default for intermediates, gold outputs and logs: typed, columnar and cheap to prune, which is why the nine session files and every pipeline log are Parquet. Writing it has a catch: lists and dicts must be normalized to JSON strings first, an explicit step in the proposals pipeline. CSV appeared in early prototypes where append-and-resume was the point, but text-heavy CSVs get big fast: 263 MB and 209 MB pipeline CSVs couldn't be parsed in a browser, so that prototype read a 5 MB pre-processed JSON. When analysts query results next to existing financial data, results belong in the database, so proposal output lands in Oracle staging tables. User state with expiry, like sessions and sign-in tokens, sits in Cosmos DB with TTL policies, and Blob Storage is the exchange layer between the server and the cloud app.

cards.answer: I want any output row traceable to its source without reading code. In the proposals pipeline, three staging tables let engineering follow a production row back through its NLP annotations to the original extracted text, and PDF metadata is saved to Parquet for audit. Every pipeline run carries a run_id shared across its stages. In the archive work, search results return the original Box path, the RIMS manifest keeps a deterministic blake2b file_uid, and reviewer decisions go to an append-only log where changing your mind adds an entry pointing at the first; 481 reviewer decisions came back stamped with the reviewer's name. In the legislative pipeline, raw model output sits beside each standardized field, the raw labeled action history is kept so the leakage guard can be re-derived, and evaluated model versions were pinned by blob digest, because re-pulling 'latest' fetches a moved tag.

cards.answer: I put heavy batch work on hardware the institution already owns and pay for cloud only where latency needs it. The proposals NLP runs entirely on the Linux server with no external API calls, so there's no per-document cost. On the legislative platform, bulk inference runs on the on-premises GPU at no marginal cost while managed cloud inference handles low-latency requests in the app. Before asking for hardware I measure: moving to vLLM recovered 6.22x throughput on the same L4, and right-sizing the language model's GPU allocation freed about 15 GB so the archival pipeline could share the server. Where cloud is the answer, I size from the workload: a written Basic versus Premium v3 analysis for a memory-bound app, and an estimated $77 a month for the procurement deployment design. The unified archival system processed 2,375 files in about 21 seconds on 4 vCPU.

cards.answer: I extract metadata from the file before asking any model about it, and I map it to a standard the receiving system already speaks. For 12,125 archival images I built a metadata pipeline with tifffile, Pillow and iptcinfo3 pulling file-level, EXIF/TIFF and IPTC fields: filename, size, format, MIME type, dimensions, resolution, compression, object name, caption and keywords. Every output field maps to IPTC Core and Dublin Core, so records move into library cataloguing systems without transformation work. The RIMS build made that a standing rule: for facts already in a file header, a model is used only to phrase them, never to discover them. Inventory metadata comes first as well. Box ingest builds the manifest from name, size, SHA-1, path and timestamps before a byte is downloaded. A metadata crosswalk is one of the open work items tracked in that build.

cards.answer: I treat a KNIME migration as removing a single point of failure, not translating nodes. The retirement workflow was lost with its KNIME server, so the Python rebuild is a modular package: configuration, warehouse extraction, panel construction, report logic, writer, output-contract validation, age adjustment, structured logging and email delivery, under one entry point and a shell runner. Every SQL query moved into version-controlled files with shared cohort CTEs. A preflight script checks the Oracle client, credentials, imports, project files, distribution list and directory permissions before the first scheduled run, not at 6 AM on a quarter boundary. Each run validates against a frozen contract of 4 files, 21 sheets and 436 columns; a float equality check that passed at 224 rows and failed at 225 became a tolerance with a printed drift. Delivery failure raises. It runs quarterly on cron in about six minutes, registered with the monitor.

cards.answer: Before any matching, I made four vendors look like one table. The procurement work grew from a single 4 MB file, where I first cleaned encoding errors and phantom columns, to six files of about 1.1 GB across four distributors, converted to Parquet and mapped into one 12-column unified schema. Manufacturer names were normalized in three passes: programmatic cleanup took 3,205 names to 2,949, blocked fuzzy clustering with rapidfuzz grouped variants without comparing every pair, and an LLM canonicalized what remained, with a five-case sanity check gating the full run and rate-limited calls on the shared server. Only after that did exact manufacturer plus part-number matching run, confirming 42,052 identical products across 6,068,888 rows.

cards.answer: The daily legislative run republishes nine per-session Parquet files to Azure gold, and the ordering is what makes that safe: hash check, conditional download, parse, label, rebuild history, rescore, build the active-bills snapshot, upload with overwrite, then save the hash. Because the hash is saved last, a run that fails before upload leaves the old hash in place and the next run reprocesses that session instead of skipping it. Whole-file overwrite keeps gold simple: each file is a complete replacement with a fixed schema (bill_id as Int64, bill_number, y_prob, n_actions, bill_year, momentum, generated_at). The app's one-hour cache TTL makes the 4 AM rescore visible the same day. A session only counted as done once gold features, Explorer metadata, FAISS index and config were verified present in Azure.

cards.answer: The 11-step chain in the proposals pipeline is as much data engineering as NLP. Step 1 loads the intermediate Parquet and validates that every row has a FILE_DATA_ID. Step 2 loads resources once, including a real-word vocabulary built from NLTK and WordNet and cached to disk, so later runs skip the rebuild. Cleaning, lemmatization and real-word filtering produce a valid-word count per document, and anything under 40 is flagged SUCCESSFULLY_PARSED=N but kept. Keyword extraction runs TF-IDF, KeyBERT in batches of 32 and LDA, then merges them. Steps 7 to 9 fit the output to the database: keyword strings truncated to 500 to 1,000 characters for column limits, and the output column schema enforced. Step 10 converts lists and dicts to JSON strings for Parquet and concatenates parsed and skipped rows. Step 11 builds the staging tables.

cards.answer: Every stage boundary writes counts, not just frames, because several defects I've caught were plausible output with the wrong number of rows behind it. The legislative pipeline takes a multi-state config.json, and the taxonomy is two tiers: 42 universal federal categories plus a state layer, with Illinois adding 21 keyword augmentations and 5 state-only categories. cards.answer: The legislative pipeline is layered Bronze, Silver, Gold: Bronze is ingested source, Silver is chunked text and LLM feature extraction, Gold is the standardized features the application reads. The layering earns its keep three ways. Isolation: during the model evaluation each configuration wrote to its own Silver paths, chunks_<profile> and features_<profile>, so no two grid cells shared state and the grid was reproducible. Recoverability: raw model output survives standardization, and keyword matching runs against the raw value first, so normalization never silently destroys a match. A clean publish boundary: Gold lives in Azure per session, with features, Explorer metadata, FAISS index and config verified before a session counts as done. Extraction happens once per bill upstream, while per-user scoring reads Gold, so adding a user never re-extracts the corpus.

cards.answer: I treat an LLM step like any other unreliable upstream: bounded input, typed output, counted failures and restartability. In the legislative pipeline, text is normalized and chunked before extraction, so a one-line amendment and a 400-page act arrive in the same shape. The model emits a 15-field structured schema parsed downstream, and each chunk carries parse_status as OK, PARTIAL or EMPTY, so parse failures are a measured rate instead of silent nulls. The extractor flushes in batches and can be killed and restarted without double-writing, which a roughly 155-hour run over 11,673 bills requires. Raw output is kept beside the standardized field. And I pin what produced it: evaluated model versions were recorded by blob digest. The research proposals pipeline keeps the LLM out for now; its semantic phase is scaffolded but not built.

on the bill passage model: what was the training population, what was held out, how was the threshold chosen, and how would the numbers change if you scored bills later in their lifecycle than introdu
cards.answer: The bill passage model is the cleanest example, because I owned every step. I framed it as a survival problem: most bills die at different procedural stages, and "will this pass" depends on when you ask. Action text was unlabeled, so I built a 47-category taxonomy and labeled 1.39 million action rows. I applied a leakage guard at one point before aggregation, expanded each bill into prefixes so the model learns from every point in its life, and split train and test at the bill level. The production model is TF-IDF into a HistGradientBoostingClassifier, rescored daily by a scheduled pipeline. Validation came last and changed the most. After a corpus correction and retraining, on a held-out General Assembly it reached 75.1% precision and 76.2% recall at a 0.70 threshold, with a median 21 days' warning.

cards.answer: The feature that moved the most was the bill itself. My introduction-time model scores a bill before any procedural history exists, and on the held-out 103rd General Assembly it sat at a near-chance ROC-AUC of 0.561. Adding each bill's title and synopsis raised it to 0.845. A jump that size makes me suspicious before it makes me happy, so I confirmed it with an ablation study and three leakage checks. The other half of feature work is removal. In the retirement model I retired the macroeconomic features: unemployment and market indices are identical for every employee in a run, so they can't change anyone's rank in a report whose whole purpose is ranking, and across 21 annual anchors they mostly let the model dress a year effect up as a market effect.

cards.answer: I validate the way the model will be used, which almost always means out of time. For bill prediction I held out an entire General Assembly, the 103rd, and split at the bill level so a bill's early actions can't sit in training while its later ones are tested. I also built safeguards so no prediction made after the outcome was known gets counted. For the retirement model, panel data of that shape must never be split at random, so splits are by anchor year only. The risk-band cut points were fitted on 2019 to 2022, frozen, then applied untouched to 2023 to 2025, and checked seven more ways by leaving one year out at a time. The Elevated band had the higher retirement rate in all seven.

cards.answer: I pick the metric that answers the stakeholder's real question, then report it against the right baseline. For bill prediction, nobody acts on an AUC. They want to know how often a call is right and how much warning it gives, so the headline is precision and recall at a 0.70 threshold plus median days of warning. For rare events I lead with PR-AUC, because ROC-AUC can look flattering when negatives dominate. The retirement model's PR-AUC is 0.182, which only means something next to a 0.024 base rate. I still use ROC-AUC where ranking is the point, as with the introduction-time bill model. And I distrust any metric without a denominator: the legacy retirement report quoted a hit rate with no false-positive count, which is close to guaranteed when you flag 12.6% of staff.

cards.answer: I treat ranking and calibration as separate claims, because a model can order people well and still print the wrong numbers. In the inherited retirement report, out-of-time testing showed the top bin predicting 42.5% where 5.6% actually retired, even though the model ranked a retiree above a non-retiree roughly 85% of the time. Stakeholders were reading those percentages literally. I replaced them with two observed-rate risk bands, Elevated at 6.3% and Lower at 0.4%, each with a 95% confidence interval. The rebuilt pipeline uses a rank-based calibration layer, and I caught that it washed out a probability floor applied before it, so the floor now runs after calibration, on the printed scale. My bill-model validation checked calibration with ECE, and the app says plainly that its probabilities rank well but run overconfident.

cards.answer: I put an interval on any comparison I'm going to act on, and I match the test to how the data is paired. In my document-intelligence evaluation every model answered the same frozen questions, so comparisons are paired: paired bootstrap intervals for effect sizes, McNemar tests for right-or-wrong outcomes, and Holm correction because I was testing many methods at once. When I later confirmed parsers, the bootstrap was clustered by source, since items from the same source are correlated. The pre-registered method, majority-of-three voting, gained 4.5 points on a 7B model with a 95% interval of 3.0 to 6.1. For proportions from small samples I use Wilson intervals and gate on the lower bound; one precision check passed at 84 of 96, 87.5%. The retirement risk bands carry 95% intervals too.

cards.answer: I design experiments so they can't reach a convenient conclusion by accident, and to be straight, my experiments have been offline evaluations, not live A/B tests on user traffic. The discipline carries over. In my document-intelligence work I froze the cases and fingerprinted every request, then pre-registered majority-of-three voting as the single confirmatory method before running the held-out set. Failed or truncated answers stayed in the denominator as zeros, and nothing was re-run to rescue a result. For the vLLM throughput study I changed one variable at a time, holding prompt design, concurrency and serving stack fixed in turn, then added a same-model control. When a vendor model scored badly, I reassessed it one mechanism at a time across 192 requests before concluding anything.

cards.answer: Small data mostly changes what I'm allowed to claim. The retirement panel has 4,891 person-year rows but only about 101 to 118 retirements, so I sized the design to the events. A three-band version looked better in-sample and collapsed under prospective testing, so the report uses two bands, and I documented that as a limit of the event count. The 75-and-over cell had zero retirements across 26 person-years, which is why I shrank those estimates toward an age-based prior. The production run aborts if the panel returns fewer than 30 positives. Evaluation sets get the same scrutiny: 80 pages couldn't rule out a 0.02 numeric-recall deficit, so a promising model counted as a lead, not a win. When pooling is possible I measure it: wider System Office data moved PR-AUC from 0.182 to 0.199.

cards.answer: I use survival framing whenever the question is about when, and the retirement forecast is the clearest case. I built annual point-in-time snapshots from 2005 onward and labeled each active person forward twelve months, a survival-style panel. For people beyond the data's support, I fitted an age-based separation hazard to published labor-force participation anchors, with a Gompertz mortality component as a floor on involuntary exit. Across 21 years, the hazard by age plus service showed Rule-of-85 eligibility behaving as a window: risk peaks approaching 85, at 19% for 80 to 85, and declines afterward. The roadmap models all departures under a competing-risks framing, roughly three times the data. Bill prediction uses the same framing; Cox proportional hazards is recorded there as future work, not something I've shipped.

cards.answer: I reach for empirical-Bayes shrinkage when a group is too small for its own estimate to be trusted. In the retirement model, a random forest returns near zero wherever it has no comparable training cases, and the 75-and-over cell had zero retirements across 26 person-years. The result was indefensible: a 74-year-old with 39 years of service scored below a 58-year-old. I built an age-adjustment module that shrinks estimates toward an age-based separation hazard, sets a floor at 60% of the age-implied hazard, counts comparable cases for each person, and caps the age-plus-service value at the range the training data supports. Every person's output shows the raw score, the prior, the support count, the shrunk value, the floor and which mechanism moved it, so a changed number can be explained from evidence.

cards.answer: Most of my forecasting has been institutional time series with short histories, so I keep the models simple and check where they fail. For UIC enrollment, my team built ARIMA models per college and student level across 14 colleges, with orders chosen by grid search and later by Auto-ARIMA on AIC and BIC. Splitting the data into Fall, Spring and Summer series removed seasonality from each one. For 12 combinations where ARIMA wouldn't give a reliable forecast, we used Holt's double exponential smoothing, sweeping alpha and beta on an 80/20 split and picking by validation RMSE. Forecasts went out as a point estimate plus or minus validation MAE. On the legislative platform, trend analysis uses 5-year monthly baselines with seasonal adjustment, regression-based trend modeling and directional momentum.

cards.answer: When I inherited the retirement-risk model, the central defect was that its "Probability of Retirement" column was never a probability. It was an ordinal ranking on an inflated scale, and out-of-time testing showed the top bin predicting 42.5% where 5.6% retired. I rebuilt it on a point-in-time panel with time-based splits, replaced the column with observed-rate bands, and told stakeholders plainly that individual values would change.

cards.answer: I use unsupervised methods mostly to find structure I didn't know to label, then hand the result to a person or a downstream rule. In the bill taxonomy work, I clustered the uncategorized remainder with TF-IDF and KMeans to name the themes the taxonomy was missing. That made coverage an iterative loop: review clusters, update the taxonomy, re-run, measure the delta. It reached 99.0%. On a 20-year email archive, LDA on subject lines found five themes, and Llama turned keyword clusters into readable topic titles; re-running on LLM summaries with 10 topics surfaced HR and compliance themes the subject lines hid. cards.answer: For predictive text features I start with sparse, inspectable representations and add semantic ones where they earn their place. The production bill model uses TF-IDF on action text, 1 to 2 grams, min_df 5, max_df 0.95, sublinear term frequency and 50,000 features, into gradient boosting. Cleaning matters as much as the vectorizer: in California, journal page numbers and legislator names were dominating the feature space until I stripped them. For research proposals I fused TF-IDF, KeyBERT and LDA keywords, since each catches what the others miss. Embeddings handle similarity: MiniLM with FAISS for archive and legislative search, bge-small over six million procurement rows. The introduction-time model leans on LLM-extracted bill semantics, and adding title and synopsis raised its held-out ROC-AUC from 0.561 to 0.845.

cards.answer: I choose by data shape and by what the model has to explain. For the bill model, 50,000 sparse TF-IDF features on action-sequence prefixes suit histogram gradient boosting: it handles interactions and stays deterministic with a fixed seed. For the retirement panel, a few thousand rows of person features, I used a 500-tree random forest, then hit its known weakness: it returns near zero wherever no comparable case exists, so it needed an age prior. Logistic regression is my interpretable baseline and fallback; the HR departure-risk design pairs it with XGBoost and falls back to eligibility and tenure rules if performance is insufficient. At UIC, H2O's random forest beat CatBoost on the class that mattered, discontinuing students. I've also run TF-IDF with KNN, logistic regression and random forest for job classification.

cards.answer: I tune in proportion to what the data can support, and I keep the search honest by validating it out of sample. For Holt's smoothing at UIC we swept alpha and beta from 0.05 to 1.0 in steps of 0.05, picked the pair with the lowest validation RMSE on an 80/20 split, then refit on all the data. ARIMA orders came from grid search, later Auto-ARIMA on AIC and BIC. For the bill model I kept a conservative, documented spec: 150 iterations, max depth 6, learning rate 0.1, min_samples_leaf 20, fixed seed. Some of the most consequential settings aren't model hyperparameters at all. I chose a 730-day recency half-life over a 5-year window with recorded reasoning, and I treated risk-band cut points as tuned parameters, frozen before testing.

cards.answer: I treat fairness as something to design and test, and I'll be precise about how far I've taken it. For the HR workforce platform I designed an equity audit view that checks whether succession and promotion recommendations are proportionally distributed across demographic groups, with top-K candidate lists reviewed for representation balance and a formal fairness review scheduled in the validation phase. That was a proof of concept on synthetic data mirroring the HR tables, so I haven't yet audited a production model on real demographic data. In production, my equity work has been about not misleading people about individuals: refusing to let retirement-risk output be labeled "projected retirements", and escalating whether the report should rank people who resemble past retirees as a business decision instead of settling it myself.

cards.answer: I monitor the inputs, the outputs and the monitor itself. The bill model runs on two clocks: a daily rescore of active bills and a monthly retrain with recency weighting, so prediction freshness and model freshness can't be confused. Pipelines write structured logs that a job execution monitor I built reads, and it alerts on failures, cascades and pipelines that go silent. The retirement pipeline validates its output against a frozen contract of 4 files, 21 sheets and 436 columns on every run, and aborts if the panel returns fewer than 30 positives. The defect that mattered most wasn't caught by a metric: stalled bills holding their peak probability showed up only once the trail was exposed. I haven't shipped a formal distribution-drift alarm; recency weighting and scheduled retraining are how I handle drift today.

cards.answer: For anomaly detection I prefer simple, explainable baselines that an analyst can check by hand. On the legislative platform, trend analysis compares activity against 5-year monthly baselines, seasonally adjusted, and flags unusual movement with Z-score anomaly detection, alongside regression-based trend modeling and directional momentum. Adjusting for season first matters, because legislative activity has a strong calendar. At the bill level, a momentum badge compares a bill's probability over its last three actions against the prior three and labels it Gaining, Stable or Losing. I apply the same idea to pipeline health: the job monitor flags a pipeline as silent when hours since its last success pass a threshold, and I set that to 100 days for a quarterly pipeline, which would otherwise breach the standard 48-hour rule two days after every run.

cards.answer: I've used Markov chains for career mobility, and it's proof-of-concept work. For the HR workforce platform, the proof of concept I led with intern collaborators built a career transition matrix from each employee's historical job-title sequence, giving the conditional probability of every next role from any starting role. A simulation engine walks those transitions stochastically and summarizes many simulated paths into a distribution of where people in a role land after N moves, for example where academic advisors end up after four moves, shown as a Sankey flow. The same matrix feeds graph analytics that classify dead-end, feeder and fast-track roles. It ran on a synthetic 500-employee dataset mirroring the HR tables. On real data, the first thing to validate is the Markov assumption that the next move depends only on the current role; the build plan schedules validation against historical trends.

cards.answer: At scale I design for vectorized passes and cheap lookups before I write a loop. Labeling 1,388,400 legislative action rows one at a time with fuzzy matching wouldn't have been runnable, so I wrote a two-pass labeler: combined regex patterns via str.contains across the whole column resolve roughly 85 to 90% of rows in under 30 seconds, then rapidfuzz partial_ratio runs only on the remainder. Final coverage was 99.65%. For procurement, a per-query DataFrame scan took about 1,700 ms, so I built an in-memory dictionary keyed on manufacturer and part number with itertuples: about 90 seconds at startup, then under 2 ms per lookup across six million rows. On the SQL side, I externalize queries into version-controlled files with shared cohort CTEs and effective-dated reads.

cards.answer: I communicate uncertainty as observed rates and plain statements people can repeat accurately. For the retirement report I replaced a fake probability with two bands and their real outcomes: in the Elevated band 6.3% retired within the year, with a 95% interval of 3.9 to 10.2, against 0.4% in the Lower band. I proposed a multi-year framing with the stakeholder, so leadership can say something defensible like a one-in-four chance of retiring within four years. I also said what the output may not be called: "projected retirements". For bill prediction I standardized one phrase, floor-vote likelihood, after finding five descriptions in the app, because someone who reads "passage" next to 94% has misunderstood before reading any documentation. UIC forecasts went out with a plus-or-minus MAE band.

The closest work is regression analysis at the San Diego Regional Data Library, quantifying differences in economic indicators between Special Economic Zone and non-zone regions, with nighttime light intensity as a proxy for economic activity. Day to day, causal thinking shows up as attribution discipline. When vLLM delivered a 6.22x speedup, I re-ran the old backend on the same model architecture to split it into 3.6x from serving and about 1.7x from the model swap. I confirm feature gains with ablations, and I keep stakeholders from reading prediction as cause: the retirement output ranks people who resemble past retirees, which is different from forecasting who will leave.

cards.answer: I evaluate LLM output like any other measurement problem: fix the bar first, sample deliberately, and report the lower bound. In Skyrule, my personal project, exhaustive grading of a 2.6-million-piece generated library would have cost about 5,600 GPU-hours, so I designed lot acceptance sampling with exact binomial plans and stated producer and consumer risk, plus code checks on every piece. Quality bars are set before measurement and reported as a point estimate and a Wilson 95% lower bound. Judges get validated too: an independent model labels claims, I measure its agreement with my own verdicts, and those labels become a regression set for the validator. In my document-intelligence evaluation, no model grades another; published answer keys and code do the scoring, and failures count as zeros.

cards.answer: A simple model is enough when it answers the decision and the extra complexity can't be validated. The bill model is TF-IDF plus gradient boosting on action-sequence prefixes. I recorded Cox proportional hazards, LSTMs and DeepSurv as an upgrade path, and documented the current approach as a deliberate baseline chosen for interpretability and production tractability. The retirement report uses two risk bands because a three-band version collapsed prospectively, and I retired macro features that added a manual quarterly chore without changing anyone's rank. In procurement, exact matching on manufacturer and part number confirmed 42,052 identical products with no AI at all; embeddings and an LLM only see what's left. A more complex method has to win out of sample before it replaces a simple one.

cards.answer: I spend more time on the target definition than on the model, because a wrong target gives a confident answer to the wrong question. For retirement risk, each annual anchor captures who was active on that date and labels them forward twelve months, with the last anchor a full year before the run so an absent retirement is a true negative. I documented the boundary cost: 4 of 122 retirements fall on the wrong side of a January-to-January window, which makes recall slightly pessimistic. At UIC we built four label variants and recommended binary success, since graduation and continuation look more like each other than like dropout. For bills, Stage 2 predicts reaching a floor vote, not becoming law, and in California I redefined the target to floor votes only.

Tree ensembles are my default for tabular data: H2O's distributed random forest at UIC and a 500-tree random forest for retirement risk. At the output level, my document-intelligence evaluation pre-registered majority-of-three voting as its confirmatory method. It held for a 7B model at plus 4.5 points and for a 32B at plus 2.6, with no reliable gain on the 8B, so it's worth its triple cost only for some models. For features, my research-proposal pipeline fuses TF-IDF, KeyBERT and LDA keywords into one profile. At UIC we documented class-sensitive ensembles for the discontinued segment as a future recommendation.

cards.answer: I staged the bill model because each point in a bill's life supports a different question. Stage 1 scores a bill at introduction, when the only signal is the bill itself. It's the hardest stage, and adding title and synopsis lifted its held-out ROC-AUC from 0.561 to 0.845. Stage 2 is the production model: given the procedural history so far, the likelihood the bill reaches a floor vote, rescored after every new action. Stage 3 predicts individual legislators' votes from vote history, party alignment and committee roles; it's trained but waiting on production feature integration before it joins the daily loop. Stage 1 activates on the server when its model file is present, with no pipeline code changes. I sequenced it with Stage 2 live and scoring daily while Stages 1 and 3 were staged for integration.

cards.answer: Most of my label sets didn't exist until I built them, so I treat label quality as something to measure. For legislative actions I labeled 1.39 million rows with procedural stage and activity type at 99.65% coverage, keeping the raw labeled history for inspection, and in California an iterative audit of unlabeled actions drove taxonomy updates. When there's no ground truth, I say so: my LLM extraction evaluation used a blind three-criterion rubric and reported no ROC curve, because rubric scores are expert judgments. I quantify boundary noise too: 4 of 122 retirement labels fall on the wrong side of the window. For institutional documents, the planned readiness gate is a human-labeled set of about 100 documents with 20 double-labeled, so agreement between labelers can be measured instead of assumed.

cards.answer: I'd explain them through mistakes I've caught. Overfitting is a model learning the sample instead of the pattern; my clearest case is a three-band retirement design that looked better in-sample and collapsed prospectively, its middle band scoring below its bottom band. That's bias versus variance in practice: with roughly a hundred events, a finer model carries more variance than the data can pay for, so I accepted the coarser two-band version. A p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme if there were no real effect, which is why testing many methods inflates false wins and why I apply Holm correction. And I watch effective sample size: recency weights are normalized to mean 1 so weighting doesn't quietly shrink the data.

cards.answer: I treat a near-perfect score as a bug report until proven otherwise, and I check four things in order. First, the target: in California the first definition counted committee votes, a 76.4% positive rate that made the task trivial, so I redefined it as floor votes only. Second, the population: my June bill model's corpus was missing every resolved bill through a status filter, and resolutions pooled with bills had inflated the success rate to 30.4% from a true 13.2%. Third, leakage and splits: outcome terms audited, bill-level splits, a full Assembly held out, and an ablation for any big feature gain. Fourth, individual behavior, because aggregates hide things: the per-action trail showed stalled bills keeping their peak probability. After the fixes I replaced the June headline with held-out results.

cards.answer: Precision at a threshold matches how the model is used: an analyst sees a flagged bill and wants to know how often a flag is right. At 0.70 on the held-out 103rd General Assembly, 75.1% of the bills the model flagged were correct calls, it caught 76.2% of the bills it should have, and the median first call came 21 days before the floor vote. The warning measure needs safeguards so no prediction made after the outcome is counted. The 0.70 itself isn't a tuned optimum. I picked it as an illustrative operating point, to show how much lead time you get at a given level of certainty, and the validation results in the platform let you choose your own threshold and see the lead time and accuracy that come with it. The right threshold depends on how many flags a team can review. And it's one held-out Assembly, which I report as such, not a long prospective record.

cards.answer: I keep a twelve-item limitations document, and four failure modes matter most. First, Stage 2 predicts reaching a floor vote, not becoming law; bills reach votes and fail, so the app says floor-vote likelihood everywhere. Second, the probability trail misbehaves after a stall: a bill that advanced and then stalled keeps its peak probability. The real fix is a decay term on time since the last advancing action plus down-weighting on re-referral, and the display patch is documented as insufficient. Third, probabilities rank well but run overconfident in absolute terms. Fourth, the evidence is one held-out Assembly, not a long prospective record. Open model work includes unifying the labeler and verifying synopses against as-introduced bill text, since Stage 1 now leans on them.

cards.answer: The biggest issue is a feature. TOTAL_COMPLETED_TERMS was the top predictor, and in October 2026 I added a correction to the case study: it counts terms across all recorded history, so it can partly reveal the outcome, and the selected model's cross-validated scores may be inflated by leakage. I'd rebuild with features computed strictly as of each snapshot, the way my retirement panel reads effective-dated rows. Second, performance varied by term: Cohen's kappa was 0.882 for Fall but 0.461 for Spring, where dropout patterns are more diffuse. Third, the SMOTE step ran without a static seed, so runs weren't deterministic. And predicted discontinued counts consistently ran under actuals, which needed an adjustment ratio. We documented those limits and recommended domain-informed feature selection.

For the rebuilt retirement-risk forecast, which Strategic Workforce Planning uses each quarter, I track three things. cards.answer: When older data is still informative but the world has shifted, I weight it instead of cutting it. For the bill model I compared a rolling 5-year training window against exponential decay and chose decay. The procedural grammar of the legislature is stable across 16 years, so a 5-year cut would discard roughly half the data for no gain; what shifts is the base rate and political salience of categories. I implemented decay as sample weights with a 730-day half-life, so a 2022 bill counts about half as much as a 2024 bill and a 2018 bill about 10%, normalized to mean 1 to preserve effective sample size. The half-life is stored in both the model artifact and the manifest, and a monthly retrain refreshes the model on full history.

cards.answer: Agents don't talk to each other in real time. They coordinate through files with owners: dependencies in the queue, dated handoff documents, a shared memory and a decision log. I chose this over agent-to-agent chat because every exchange then leaves a record that a new session, a reviewer or I can read later, and nothing depends on two agents being awake at once. A job can name the jobs it waits for, so one department's output becomes another's input without polling. cards.answer: Agent City is a read-mostly projection: it owns no scheduling and runs no work. One pure function turns a few authoritative fields into one state with fixed precedence: blocked, waiting on me, working, queued, offline, paused, scheduled soon, sleeping, idle. Unreachable means offline, never asleep. Browsers poll every 5 seconds with a cursor; I chose polling over push for simplicity. Run now sets aside one date gate and never overrides approvals, dependencies, a usage pause or the budget. Commands are previewable, and the same key within 24 hours returns the stored result. The Done log holds 1,060 finished jobs, and the town is reachable only over my private network.

cards.answer: I design it as a funnel where every stage can be checked on its own. Ingest with a stable ID per document, so any answer traces back to its source; in the archive search the Box file_id rides through all eight stages. Chunk to the size the model handles well, which I measure rather than assume. Embed with one model, L2-normalize, and pick the FAISS index for the scale. Retrieve with a calibrated threshold plus structured filters, so the LLM only sees a few dozen candidates. For citations I don't let the model quote. In Evidence Desk the model returns block IDs and the label, and code copies the exact text and checks its hash, which removed every copy failure. I measure retrieval coverage separately, because when the right block never arrives, no prompt can fix it.

cards.answer: I use hybrid retrieval whenever exact signals exist, because vectors are good at meaning and weak on identifiers. In procurement the exact tier, a dictionary keyed on manufacturer and part number, answers in under 2ms and always runs; FAISS covers only what it misses, since semantic matches alone carry too many false positives for numbers people will act on. In the HERDS classifier I blend a semantic score with a keyword-overlap score at 0.75 to 0.25, which beat either signal alone on the validation set, with a 0.12 floor before any label is assigned. The legislative platform pairs MiniLM and FAISS search with structured filters and keyword matching on raw extracted text. I haven't run BM25 itself in production; I'd tune its weight the same way, on labeled queries.

cards.answer: I pick the index for the scale and the recall I need. For the legacy archive, thousands of summaries, I used IndexFlatIP over L2-normalized MiniLM embeddings, so inner product equals cosine and search is exact; the HNSW version persists to disk and loads instantly with no database server. At 5.19 million product vectors, about an 8GB index, exhaustive search stops making sense, so procurement uses IVFFlat with 4,096 lists and nprobe 64, returning candidates in 75 to 110ms. nprobe is the recall dial: probe more lists for better recall and slower queries. I build indexes offline once and rebuild only when descriptions change, not prices. And I keep vectors out of the main table: at five million rows, 384-dimension embeddings are roughly 7.5 GB that almost nothing reads.

cards.answer: Most throughput problems I've seen live in the serving layer. On our L4, Ollama handled one request at a time: throughput stayed flat at about 9 images a minute from concurrency 1 to 8 while p50 latency rose 8.18x and the GPU sat at 28 to 31%. vLLM's continuous batching took the same card to 55.4 images a minute at concurrency 8 and 96 to 97% utilization. The KV cache is the next limit. Mistral with 3,000-token chunks saw p99 grow from 15s to 74s between concurrency 1 and 24, head-of-line blocking from cache pressure, so it was dropped. I choose the operating point by sweeping concurrency: for Llama 3.1 8B, quality held within 0.6 points from 1 to 24, so 12 to 24 became purely a throughput and latency call.

cards.answer: I budget VRAM as weights plus KV cache plus runtime overhead, then check the real allocation. AWQ is how a 7 to 8B model fits our 22.5 GB L4 with room to batch: about 4 GB at idle, leaving roughly 18 GB for KV cache and co-resident pipelines. On my personal RTX 5090 I serve AWQ and FP8 models through vLLM, Qwen3 32B AWQ among them, and I sized a context change from 4,096 to 16,384 tokens with KV-cache arithmetic and a benchmark before adopting it. Two lessons came from failures. Ollama's keep_alive held about 6 GB and blocked vLLM's cache allocation, and right-sizing one model's allocation freed about 15 GB so the archival pipeline could share the server. The format matters too: the same 32B model accepted 3 groups on vLLM with AWQ and 1 on Ollama with Q4_K_M.

cards.answer: I write the SLO down before the run and project it against the real corpus, not the test sample. For the legislative pipeline the 50-state target was about 75,000 bills a week in an 18-hour processing window: 1.157 bills a second sustained, 2.41 at peak. Llama 3.1 8B on one L4 measured 0.88 chunks a second at concurrency 24; at 2.40 chunks per bill on the real length distribution, that's 0.367 bills a second. That passes the Illinois workload with 2.05x headroom and misses the national target by 3.16x, so the hardware ask became specific: about three L4s or one A100-class card for steady state, about seven L4s or H100-class hardware for bursts. I track p99 as well as the mean, because the tail is what blocks a batch queue.

cards.answer: I treat a prompt like code with a version, because a silent prompt edit invalidates every comparison after it. In Skyrule, my personal project, the generation prompt gets a new immutable id on every change, and in the document evaluation any new prompt or variant became a new protocol version with its own frozen cases. The extraction schemas I design carry model-version and prompt-version columns, so every stored value says what produced it. On the craft side, I bundle related questions in one prompt so earlier answers give context to later ones, state rejection rules explicitly, and ask for output only, with no preamble. When a validator rejected acceptable text in a Skyrule pilot, fixing the prompt and the check together raised plan acceptance from 6 of 31 to 14 of 31.

cards.answer: I build the evaluation so the numbers can't drift between runs. Cases are frozen and hashed before any model sees them; every request, client setting and scorer is fingerprinted, and the merge tool refuses rows that fail the check. That's how two machines, two coding assistants and weeks of runs produced 40,975 scored rows in one report. Scoring is code against answer keys wherever a key exists: character error, TEDS, relaxed accuracy, numeric recall. Failures and truncations stay in the denominator as zero. I use a model as grader only where judgment can't be computed, and I check it first: two independent Opus passes agreed on 60 of 60 cells, and Skyrule's grader must clear 85% agreement at the Wilson lower bound. Regression means rerunning the same frozen suite and comparing cell by cell.

In my October evaluation, Qwen3-VL 8B on a 12 GB laptop read prose crops at about 1.2% character error, matching the 32B models. On fresh financial tables the small PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 parser beat Qwen3-VL 32B, 0.852 against 0.762 TEDS. cards.answer: My rule is to do everything deterministic before any model runs, then send each task to the cheapest model that clears its bar. Procurement is the clearest example: an exact dictionary lookup on manufacturer and part number answers in under 2ms, FAISS narrows six million rows to a median of 44 candidates in 75 to 110ms, and only then does a 7B model judge equivalence, in 5 to 8 seconds. If the LLM is offline, the exact tier still returns. The archival build follows the same order: free filters first, and no file reaches enrichment unless triage selected it. In Skyrule, my personal project, routing comes from measurement on my own GPU: Claude models for design, review and audit, local Qwen models for bulk generation and grading, small models for utilities.

cards.answer: I cache at three levels: model responses, expensive artifacts and computed results. Procurement caches LLM responses by prompt hash, so a repeated query costs nothing. Indexes and embeddings are built offline once: FAISS indexes live as files on disk, the research pipeline caches its taxonomy embeddings and vocabulary, and browse categories are pre-indexed at API startup in about 30 seconds so browsing is instant. On the legislative platform, live impact scoring is cache-first: each bill and prompt pair is scored once and read instantly after, and nightly rescoring uses content hashes so only changed bills are re-evaluated. Streamlit data loads sit behind st.cache_data with a one-hour TTL, so the 4 AM rescore shows up the same day. Every cache has an explicit invalidation key: prompt hash, content hash or TTL.

cards.answer: I design every write so a rerun is harmless and every failure is bounded. The research proposals pipeline inserts with WHERE NOT EXISTS or MERGE, checks the row count it wrote against what it attempted and raises if they differ, and prints the exact rollback SQL on every run. Long jobs checkpoint and resume rather than restart: the legislative extractor flushes in batches and can be killed without double-writing. Retries need a ceiling. One malformed bill truncated, failed to parse, was never written, reappeared as new and failed again for six days; the fix was a length guard plus a retry limit that parks the record instead of reprocessing it forever. My job queue gives three attempts by default and flags runs that exceed a time limit set per lane.

cards.answer: I monitor for absence as much as for errors, because AI pipelines usually fail quietly. Every pipeline writes the same Parquet log schema, with PIPELINE_START and PIPELINE_END sentinel rows sharing a run ID; a start with no end, or no successful run inside the window, raises a silent-pipeline alert. Root failures are separated from the cascade they cause, and only critical ones send email, so alerts stay readable. Then I audit the monitor itself. On the legislative pipeline a stage reported success while producing zero output, so completion now requires a non-zero count, and alert delivery turned out never to be verified. Quarterly jobs get their own silence threshold, 2,400 hours with matching Grafana panels, instead of alerting for 89 days straight.

cards.answer: I anonymize in two layers so the LLM never has to be the privacy control. In the email archive, Microsoft Presidio first detects structured PII such as names, phone numbers, emails and SSNs, and replaces it with typed placeholders like <PERSON1>, keeping the mapping separately. Then a local Llama 3.2 model writes a summary, instructed to generalize any remaining personal detail. Placeholder text produced more coherent summaries than raw text with names still in it. The model runs locally through Ollama. The failure to watch for is over-redaction: in the RIMS build the redaction layer labeled ZIP+4 codes as social security numbers and chart axis labels as card numbers, which would have stripped research data from the reading-room copy. So I check what gets removed, not only what survives.

cards.answer: I start by asking whether the inputs, the infrastructure or the model changed, and I check output volume and shape before trusting a green status. Three real cases. cards.answer: I choose by data sensitivity, volume and latency. Ollama is simple to run and fine for one request at a time, but on our L4 it serialized requests. vLLM is what I use for volume, because continuous batching took the same card from about 9 to 55.4 images a minute; on an air-gapped server I staged the weights by hand to get it. cards.answer: I sample GPU utilization, VRAM and power in the same window as the workload, because averages from separate runs hide the signature I'm looking for. cards.answer: I moved to vLLM because the measurements said the server was the bottleneck: Ollama held throughput flat across concurrency with the L4 28 to 31% busy, so a bigger GPU would have bought nothing. The server is air-gapped, and curl -v showed the block was specific: GitHub, PyPI and the Ollama registry worked, HuggingFace died at the TLS handshake. Three things broke in the 0.6.6 stand-up: mistral_common had moved an import, transformers was a major version ahead, and Ollama's keep_alive held about 6 GB that vLLM's KV cache needed. cards.answer: Each alternative failed a specific stage that Llama passed. On parse-OK, Llama 3.1 8B led at every chunk size, 85.0 to 92.5%, peaking at 1,200 tokens, while no Mistral or Qwen cell reached 73%. A blind rubric review on 60 cells confirmed the ranking. Qwen went out because its own parse-OK misranked its chunk sizes; its peak was valid JSON full of None. Mistral went out on the tail: with 3,000-token prompts its p99 grew from 15s to 74s by concurrency 24 under KV cache pressure. A 14B model given whole bills scored 45.0%. At 1,200 tokens the median bill of 1,051 tokens is one chunk, and quality held within 0.6 points from concurrency 1 to 24, so 12 to 24 is where the GPU is used well.

I iterated the validator through seven versions from my own reviews, adding checks for truncated claims, causal leaps, wrong-person attribution and contradictions. Each new check must catch the defects I named (8 of 8 in v7), report its false-alarm rate on previously accepted claims, and survive mutation testing, 21 of 21 deliberate breaks caught. Checks can be too strict: an over-literal one rejected good text, and fixing it raised plan acceptance from 6 to 14 of 31. Canary 1 failed its check at 18 of 50, so five wording habits became new checks before any full run.

cards.title: What breaks first at 10x scale

cards.answer: GPU throughput breaks first, and I know by how much. The 50-state target is about seven times Illinois volume, and one L4 running Llama 3.1 8B at concurrency 24 falls 3.16x short of the steady-state SLO and 6.57x short of peak burst. Next is the length tail: 12% of bills exceed 10,000 tokens and the longest is over a million, so chunk counts per bill, and KV cache pressure if chunks grow, rise faster than bill counts. Uniform chunking is the next thing I'd change, with adaptive tiers by bill length. On the app side, memory already bit once: semantic search failed under memory pressure until the tier moved to Premium v3 and loads became selective. The data pipeline itself scales, because ingestion is hash-based and only changed sessions download.

cards.answer: I split by who is waiting and what it costs. On the legislative platform, heavy work runs as batch on institution-owned GPU: nightly feature extraction and impact scoring on vLLM, at no marginal cost, with nobody waiting. User-facing requests go to managed inference on Azure OpenAI, where latency matters. The two meet in one result schema. A user's prompt against a single bill can be scored live, stored and read instantly afterward, and the nightly batch writes the same long-format table, one row per user, prompt and bill, so either path can fill a cell. The split began as a workaround when the campus network blocked the server from the database, and became a deliberate design. Features are extracted once per bill, so adding a user never re-extracts the corpus.

cards.answer: I treat the token budget as part of the design, because truncation fails quietly. When Qwen 2.5 14B got whole 5,000-token bills, too little room was left to finish an 11-field JSON: 54% of outputs were partial, averaging 1.2 missing fields, with zero outright failures. In the document evaluation every task had a fixed budget, from 300 to 6,000 tokens, and a truncated answer scored zero instead of being rerun with more room. That rule exposed a thinking build that spent its budget on hidden reasoning, so it was removed. A hosted model first tested at a 600-token budget truncated; raising the budget alone changed nothing, while enabling reasoning did. For user-written profile context, I set explicit length limits and explained them to users.

cards.answer: I validate a cheap metric against a careful one before I tune on it. Parse-OK rate, the share of outputs that parse into every field, is fast and scales, so I tested it twice on the legislative sweep. Across models it held: a blind rubric review on 60 cells ranked the three models the same way, and two independent scoring passes agreed on all 60. Within a model it failed. In every informative pair the smaller chunk size scored at least as well on substance, even where parse-OK disagreed, because larger chunks produced confident answers about the wrong section of the bill. For Qwen, the parse-OK peak was valid JSON full of the string None. So parse-OK ranks models for me, and chunk sizes need substantive review.

cards.answer: Eight stages joined by one manifest, each with a named owner, a gate condition that defines done, and a stated dependency on the stage before it: 00 source and access, 01 inventory and identify, 02 triage and appraisal, 03 extraction and routing, 04 enrichment, 05 metadata, 06 index, search and delivery, 07 scale and scheduling. The manifest is one row per file path, stored as partitioned Parquet, and each stage adds the columns it owns, which is what makes a mixed accession processable at all. Inside extraction, files go down format lanes, email, image, document, tabular and scientific, rather than one path. My standing rule there: where a fact is already in a file header, a model only phrases it, never discovers it. The September 2026 demonstration processed 2,375 real files across three accessions in about 21 seconds on 4 vCPU, with the review interface on top.

cards.answer: Find the shared representation first, then remove the dependencies that can't scale. The archival production build merged three proofs of concept, image classification, email processing and file search, which had three corpora and no shared vocabulary. The unifying piece is a single manifest every stage reads and writes. Then I treated blockers as design inputs. The file-search prototype drove Word, Excel and PowerPoint through COM automation, which can't run on Colab or the Linux GPU server, can't be parallelized safely and hangs on malformed files, so porting to Tika plus headless LibreOffice is a prerequisite, with output parity checked against the prototype on the same files. The image work's throughput limit came off first: moving to vLLM took a full 12,125-image pass from about 22 hours to about 3.7. Each inherited prototype folder also got a README saying what's reusable and what's known to be broken.
