cards.answer: Honestly, I haven't built a multi-organization SaaS. The legislative platform serves one institution with per-user isolation inside it. Cosmos DB holds each user's profile, tracked bills, categories, impact prompts and scores under a partition-key schema shared by the live app and the nightly scorer. The move that makes it scale per user is decoupling: bill features are extracted once per bill, and impact scoring runs per user against their own prompts, so adding a user never re-extracts the corpus. Sharing is explicit, team-wide versus named individual, and every AI briefing is bound to the user whose lens produced it. The closest thing to multi-tenant design is Legacy, a personal project, where every record carries a userId and every storage path is user-scoped, so opening it to other users is an additive change.

cards.answer: I run 29 agents across Skyrule and my other personal projects on one workstation with one GPU (as of October 2026), organized like a small company: each has a written charter saying what it owns and what it doesn't. They share four rails: one job queue, one memory, one decision log and an ownership map that tooling enforces. The queue is the only thing that launches work, so "why did this run now?" always has one logged answer; the cost is that the queue becomes critical infrastructure, so I kept it small, file-based and tested. Lanes are statements about shared resources, each with its own concurrency limit: 4 for CPU scripts, 1 for vLLM because speed comes from batched requests inside a run, and a budgeted Claude lane. Jobs carry dependencies, start conditions and finish checks that decide done by evidence rather than exit code.

cards.answer: I make the GPU a lease with exactly one holder. In my personal agent system, a vLLM server reserves 94% of the RTX 5090 and a 32B Ollama seat needs about 20 GB, so they can't share, and when they collide Ollama doesn't fail loudly; it spills to the CPU and runs about ten times slower. So the card is idle, one vLLM profile, or the Ollama seats, never two. A switch never interrupts running GPU work: it's refused and asked again on the next tick. After every switch the result is checked against actual memory use and server health, never assumed. Time windows for who holds the card, generation overnight and agents by day, still run as a dry run. Evidence Desk follows the same rule at work: one model resident on the GPU at a time.

cards.answer: Drop Radar, a personal project, improves itself from its user's texts, and the architecture is a loop with gates. Anything sent to the Telegram bot that isn't a command is saved to a feedback inbox. A file watcher notices a new note, or a source that has started failing, and queues a run of a dedicated Claude Code agent with written rules and a living knowledge file. The agent diagnoses the issue, edits the code or source configuration, runs the tests, restarts the service and replies with what changed. The gates: 25 tests on fabricated data, a live on and off flag for every extra feature so anything declined comes out without a restart, and a weekly check-in with Keep, Change and Drop buttons per change. One bug taught me the watcher must compare note identities, not counts: a new note went unnoticed because the open count hadn't changed.

cards.title: Model lifecycle: two clocks, auto-pickup and one input path
questions: how do you architect retraining and rescoring

cards.answer: I separate prediction freshness from model freshness and run them as two independent clocks. For bill passage prediction, a daily run rescores active bills through the current model as new actions land, and a monthly retrain refreshes the model on full history with recency weights. The daily job picks up a new model file automatically, no code change, and the introduction-time model was built the same way: it activates on the server when its model file is present. Conflating the two clocks means either stale predictions or needless retraining. Inputs go through one shared module used by both training and nightly scoring, after I found the two formatting inputs differently; 36,028 inputs now verify byte-identical. And versions get pinned: re-pulling a moved "latest" tag silently changes the model you evaluated.

cards.answer: I'd start from three decisions: what it may see, who it answers for, and how a reader checks it. On the legislative platform, retrieval is hybrid, MiniLM embeddings in FAISS alongside structured filters, and the Legislative Assistant, built on Microsoft's Copilot agent framework with GPT-4.1, returns citation-backed, structured answers. I set the retrieval standards up front, embedding selection, metadata indexing and incremental updates, along with citation and interpretability requirements for executive trust. Who it answers for is a profile: each user's title, functional area, stakeholders and interests are injected into the prompt, so the same bill reads as a budget issue for one person and an AI-ethics question for another. For sensitive collections, my archival version 2 design keeps everything local: a 30B-class model on vLLM, BGE-M3 embeddings, FAISS or Qdrant, no external calls.

cards.answer: I designed it around a governance risk identified in advance: an AI characterizing a named colleague's position slightly wrong, inside a FOIA-able system, at a public university. So the architecture holds a hard line between human and AI attribution. Every machine-generated briefing is badged as AI-authored and bound to the user whose lens produced it, so a model's interpretation is never mistaken for a colleague's stated position. Shares are team-wide or to a named individual, the distinction is stored and shown, and individual shares and flags sort above broadcasts. Imports can be untracked reversibly, so a mistake costs no data. The mitigation adopted is that users own and can correct any extracted characterization of their own view before others see it, and those corrections double as training signal for the planned institutional-memory capability.

cards.answer: I sort roadmap work by adoption cost, and I look hard for the schema decisions that are free now and prohibitively expensive later. On the legislative platform the clearest one is attribution: extraction must bind every claim to a person, a timestamp and the verbatim source sentence from day one, because reconstructing who held which position after the fact would mean reprocessing the entire corpus. Second, position records as the durable artifact. Discussion is raw material; what gets retrieved years later is the institutional position, the reasoning, who was in the room and what changed their mind. Third, for the planned digest agent, I framed the deployment choice, precomputed nightly on on-prem vLLM versus generated live on managed cloud inference, as the gating architectural decision rather than an implementation detail.

cards.answer: Ask for the smallest behavior change possible and let existing infrastructure do the routing. For the legislative platform I designed per-bill dossiers fed by an intake mailbox that users simply CC. The institution's most valuable legislative analysis already lives in email threads and is lost when those threads are archived. Inbound mail would be matched to the right bill through the platform's existing semantic matching, and email carries sender identity for free, so every contribution arrives attributed. Pointing the same mailbox at the clerk's committee postings turns a manual phone-call process into a push feed for hearing alerts: one mechanism for two of the three most-cited stakeholder pain points. To be clear, it's designed and on the roadmap, scoped in follow-up meetings, not built yet.

cards.answer: Where judgment is needed, and at the coarsest level that still works. For the archival pipeline's version 2, I scoped a fully local agent that scans an ingested drive, builds an understanding of the owner's subject domain, and ranks files for archival value, sensitivity and review priority with written explanations an archivist can evaluate. The constraint I wrote into version 1: agent loops belong at folder and collection level, not per file, because an agent loop costs many model calls where a classification costs one, and at corpus scale that's hours versus weeks. Anything a deterministic step or a single classification can do stays outside the agent; if the task doesn't require interpreting something undefined, it isn't agent work. The proposed stack stays on the network: a 30B-class model on vLLM, a vision-language model, BGE-M3, FAISS or Qdrant, controlled filesystem access.

cards.answer: A few, all from things that bit me. My agent job queue keeps over a thousand jobs in one JSON file guarded by a lock file and rewrites the whole list on every change; I'd use SQLite from day one. It detects usage limits by matching text in job output, which once paused a lane for a day when an agent's own report mentioned the limit; the real fix is a structured exit signal. Shell writes are guarded by heuristics, so I'd run each agent in a sandbox where out-of-scope paths simply aren't writable. On the legislative pipeline I'd make success falsifiable from the start: a stage could report green with zero output, and one malformed bill looped as a poison pill for six days. And the probability trail's monotonicity fix belongs in the model, not the display layer.

cards.answer: I gate by consequence: the more public or irreversible the action, the closer the gate sits to a person. The legislative digest shipped behind a dry-run flag and a test-recipient redirect, and go-live waited for in-person onboarding. In my personal agent system I wrote down three authority levels: agents fix isolated bugs alone, a department head approves bounded changes, and only I decide spending, release scope, sensitive data and public deployment. No agent publishes; the shell guard denies every git push. Release steps are receipt-gated, so each starts only when its predecessor's receipt carries the exact result the gate reads. At work, the archival program-manager agent holds proposed GitHub updates for human review.

cards.title: A reference architecture for a first production LLM system
questions: what reference architecture would you propose for a company's first production llm system

cards.answer: Assembled from what has worked for me. Start with a small open model on one owned GPU behind vLLM with an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and a config-driven router so the backend can change without code changes. Put deterministic code in front: exact matches, hash-based change detection, cheap filters, so the model only sees what survives. Store artifacts as Parquet with one schema contract per stage, and make every write idempotent and resumable. Route by sensitivity, volume and latency: sensitive and bulk work local, small interactive calls to a managed API, with results cached per input. Let code copy evidence and compute numbers; the model picks and judges. Give every job a standard log schema and a monitor that checks output counts, not exit codes. Ship behind dry-run flags and test recipients, and measure on your own documents before anyone calls it accurate.

cards.answer: With 29 agents and hundreds of jobs, logs stopped answering "who is working, who is stuck, who is waiting on me?", so I built Agent City, a personal project: a 3D town in the browser that is a read-mostly projection of the real system. It owns no scheduling and runs no work. Each agent carries a few authoritative fields, and one pure function maps them to a single displayed state with fixed precedence: blocked, waiting on me, working, queued, offline, paused, scheduled soon, sleeping, idle. An unreachable runtime shows as offline, never asleep, and tests check every conflicting pair, so "working" means a job is actually running. Browsers poll every 5 seconds with a cursor, which is simple and holds up on a standard-library server. Separately, an hourly Overseer round checks every agent for failed, stuck or vanished runs, and never acts.

cards.answer: Every control in a UI has to pass the same gates as everything else. In Agent City, my personal agent dashboard, "run now" sets aside one date gate on one queued job and records the original; it's refused for approval flags, dependencies and start conditions, and it never overrides a usage pause or the launch budget. Every command can be previewed without changing anything. Commands that spend usage, override a gate, pause or cancel need an explicit confirm. The same idempotency key within 24 hours returns the stored result and never creates a second job, so a double tap on a phone is harmless. Running jobs are never touched. The town's few writes go through the queue's own lock, and because queue records can be pruned or rewritten, the town appends each finished job once to an append-only Done log. Access is private-network only.

cards.answer: For long, expensive generation runs I chain steps on receipts, not on exit codes. In Skyrule, my personal project, every chain step starts only when its predecessor's receipt JSON carries the exact result the gate reads, so a failed step can't be run past. Releases go through a quarantined canary on a frozen, dated protocol with acceptance gates set in advance. Canary 1 failed its 50-piece two-grader check at 18 of 50, and the five generator habits behind it became validator checks. A supervisor with a wall-clock backstop stops generation at a cutoff, verifies the model server is down and restores the standing server, while a connection watch attributes every client touching the model port by Windows job-object membership. Each verification is bound to the code hashes it tested, so an old pass can't open a gate after a change.

cards.answer: I design outputs so a person can argue with them, which usually means storing the reason next to the result. The legislative passage model writes a per-action probability trail, 432,262 rows, as a first-class artifact rather than one score per bill. The trail drives the in-app curve and the momentum badge, which compares the last three actions with the prior three, and it exposed a monotonicity defect that a single current value would have hidden. In the archival triage ledger, every file shows why it ranked where it did, quoted from the archivist's own intake form, and folder-level inclusion stays a separate stated reason rather than being blended into one number. The retirement forecast emits per-person explainability: raw score, age prior, comparable cases, the shrunk estimate, the floor, and which mechanism moved it.

cards.answer: I design for the hours nobody's watching, which mostly means honest launches and honest health. In my personal projects, jobs launch only from the scheduled task, never from a chat session, after a session-launched job died with its console. Drop Radar's loop stopped twice in one day because the scheduled task opened a visible console that a stray Ctrl+C could kill, so it moved to a hidden launcher with an auto-restart wrapper. Health has to mean it worked: the Discord feed counts as healthy only if a post actually arrived in the last 24 hours, and a watcher raises a Telegram alarm when no source has been checked for 30 minutes; it fired 34 minutes into a real outage. A periodic hook may queue work only from an allowlist of scripts and arguments, at most hourly, so editing config can't run an arbitrary command.

cards.title: Building human review into the pipeline: the Accession Workbench
questions: how do you architect human review into an ai pipeline

cards.answer: Review is part of the architecture, so it gets a real surface and a real record. The archival pipeline's Accession Workbench puts a triage ledger in front of the archivist: every file shows its generated title, a two-sentence summary, folder location, flags and its ranking reason. Decisions can be made per file or a whole band at a time, with sensitive material automatically excluded from bulk actions. Decisions go into an append-only log, where changing your mind writes a second entry pointing at the first, because "selected at 14:02, changed at 14:19" is the record an archive needs. Three release versions, original, reading room and open web, sit side by side, so the archivist chooses what publishes rather than trusting a setting. A review pass returned 481 decisions, each stamped with its reviewer, and exposed a real rationale-field bug.

cards.title: Scaling the archival pipeline: compute, layout and agent cost
questions: what breaks first when the archive pipeline scales
scaling the archival pipeline to millions of files

why are embeddings stored outside the manifest

sizing the archival workload

cards.answer: Scale shows up in three places: compute, data layout and agent cost. Compute: under Ollama a full 12,125-image pass took about 22 hours; on vLLM with the same L4 it takes about 3.7, and a 100,000-image collection moves from 12 to 13 days to about 30 hours with no new hardware. Data layout: at five million rows, 384-dimension embeddings are about 7.5 GB, so they live outside the manifest as pointers, and building roughly a hundred columns one at a time fragments the DataFrame, harmless at five rows and severe at five million. Agent cost: loops belong at folder and collection level, because per-file loops turn hours into weeks. And the biggest lever, the free-filter reduction, has to be measured on a complete drive before any of this sizing is trusted.

cards.answer: For Skyrule, my personal project, the hosting plan follows one rule: valuable machinery stays server-side. The decided plan is a stateless FastAPI container on a DigitalOcean droplet with managed PostgreSQL, the web front end on Vercel, Clerk and Stripe, and an iOS app that's a thin client. The IP-protection plan backs that up with per-account rate limits, traceable delivery logs and trade-secret practice, informed by research I ran on client decompilation, API scraping and model distillation. The internal API is locked down on a reviewed branch: authentication on every route, no prompt or rule-file exposure, closed CORS, rate limits. Privacy shapes the data layer too: users' personal chart data never goes to a cloud model, consent gates storing anyone else's data, and the database plan includes deletion and export. It's pre-beta, so this is decided architecture, not yet load-tested.

cards.title: Content addressing and hashing as an architecture tool
questions: how do you use hashing in your architectures
content addressing
deterministic file ids blake2b
content hash change detection
fingerprinting requests and scorers
how do you know two runs used the same inputs
stable identifiers across re crawls
hash based incremental processing
why hash everything
sha 256 receipts
proving two runs were the same test
cards.answer: I use hashes wherever "is this the same thing?" has to be answered by code. In the archival manifest, file_uid is a blake2b hash over source identifier plus normalized path, so a re-crawl yields identical keys and manifest generations join; exact duplicates collapse by content hash in the free-filter tier but stay recorded as duplicate_of rather than deleted. The legislative pipeline's change feed is a content hash per artifact, so a quiet day does almost no work, and nightly impact scoring re-evaluates only bills whose hash changed. Evidence Desk fingerprints frozen case manifests, requests, client settings and scorers with SHA-256, and the merge tool refuses anything that doesn't match. In my personal agent system, every memory stores its source file's hash, and gate passes are bound to the code hashes they tested.

cards.answer: A digest is a scheduled assembly job over a user's own lens, so the lens is data and the schedule is a function. On the legislative platform a timer-triggered Azure Function assembles each recipient's digest from their profile, impact prompts, saved categories and tracked bills, and delivers it through managed email on their chosen cadence: daily, weekly or real-time. I designed the structure as state over time: headline finding, baseline framing, tracked bills, other movers, most imminent items, the macro picture, and a count of watched items with no material change. The first edition establishes a baseline and later editions report only what changed. The next design step is a digest agent that curates by reasoning across all of a user's signals instead of filtering on thresholds, where the deciding question is nightly on-prem precompute versus live cloud generation.

cards.title: Skyrule's system architecture: code computes, the model writes
questions: walk me through skyrule's architecture

how do you keep an llm from inventing facts in a product

cards.answer: Skyrule, my personal project, is layered so that anything factual is computed by code and the model only writes. At the bottom is a deterministic Python engine exposed through a versioned FastAPI layer, with regression controls that must reproduce 279 reference spans exactly. Above it is a rule store built by a provenance pipeline over a 76-title licensed corpus: extraction, independent verification by a second model, a verbatim-quote gate and page re-checks, so every rule traces to a book, a page and a quote. The relationship model is explicit functions with 206 weights held in a ledger, deliberately producing no total or compatibility score. Generation is brief-then-prose: code lays out what's supported, a local model plans claim by claim, code validates every claim, then the model writes one sentence per approved claim and code checks again.

cards.answer: I treat one shared server as a platform with conventions, because several production pipelines run on it at once: legislative processing, proposal NLP, archival image classification, the retirement forecast and more. Each gets its own environment. vLLM 0.6.6 lives in an isolated conda environment because the system Python carries a different vLLM and an incompatible syntax surface, so serving runs in the vLLM environment and the benchmark scripts in system Python; the retirement forecast runs in its own virtual environment. Every pipeline writes the same Parquet logging contract, so one monitor sees all of them. Shared resources get managed explicitly: right-sizing the language model's GPU allocation freed about 15 GB so the archival pipeline could share the L4, and after an out-of-memory failure took down the shared JupyterHub, I moved heavy jobs off it.

cards.answer: On October 26 I folded Skyrule's 14 agent departments into five working teams: Foundation, Platform, App & Brand, Release and Program. The goal was fewer deciders, with records staying in their department homes. The departments survive as review hats, and each team's write scope is generated as the union of the hats it wears, never wider; the agent-definition folder and the live site stay out of every team's scope. I tested the change like code: 31 build checks including a planted out-of-scope control, guard self-tests at 45 of 45 and 27 of 27, and 12 live allow and deny checks. Alongside it came an append-only status log with a single locking writer, self-tested with four writers appending 25 lines at once and none interleaved, a daily morning-brief PDF built from files with no model, and a 30-minute stall watch.

cards.answer: I treat model usage as a shared resource with its own lane and its own ledger. In my personal agent system the Claude lane spends my own usage, so it's opt-in per job: a job without an approval note never starts there. A weekly budget, enforced by the queue from its own launch log, caps launches so at least half my weekly usage stays free for my own work, and every raise is recorded with my reason. Unattended Claude jobs are capped at two at a time, while the GPU and CPU lanes are unmetered. When Claude reports a usage limit, the whole lane pauses until the stated reset, and that stop doesn't count as a failed attempt. The gap I'd close: cost is tracked as launches against the budget, not as tokens.

cards.answer: I started from a premise: a single institution-wide impact score is too broad to act on, because impact only means something relative to a person's role. So on the legislative platform each user defines a lens and the system applies it to every active bill. The profile, title, functional area, stakeholders served and the legislation they watch for, is injected into the LLM prompt for every downstream analysis. Users write impact questions in their own words, and each is scored against every active bill on a No, Low, Moderate or High scale with a one-sentence rationale. Up to ten keyword categories each choose which fields they search. I built explicit token and input-length limits into the profile and prompt interfaces so user-written context can't silently truncate the model's input, and explained the reason to users.

cards.answer: I put it where the team already talks and kept every write behind review. For the archival build I set up a shared program-manager agent in Microsoft Teams to track progress and blockers and link chat updates to GitHub issues, with proposed GitHub updates held for human review before anything changes. I drafted its acceptance criteria: shared access, reading a designated chat, accurate issue matching, duplicate prevention and reviewed GitHub updates. Then I report against them honestly. It opens in Teams, and GitHub issue retrieval and designated-chat retrieval have been demonstrated; automatic monitoring, persistent duplicate prevention and GitHub writes remain unverified. It sits on a repository built as the single source of truth, with 33 open issues across stages 00 to 07 and Blocked as a board column rather than a label.

cards.title: How I assess AI readiness: the 0 to 4 method
questions: how do you assess an organization's ai readiness

cards.answer: I score readiness per table, not per organization, because the question is whether people and AI tools can use each table correctly today. Every table gets one level: 0 undocumented, 1 described, 2 usable, 3 governed, 4 AI-ready, and it only reaches a level when it passes every check for that level and those below. Most checks are deterministic, so code scores them the same way every time: description coverage, placeholder or encoding-damage flags, a stated grain, documented keys and join paths, coded columns linked to a lookup, a named owner, usage rules such as validity windows, and for level 4, entry in the semantic layer plus verified questions that pass. Priority is value times gap, with value taken from query logs and dependent reports. The output is a ranked work list per owner. Status: research done, prototype scorer next.

cards.answer: Not until there's a semantic layer under it. These tools are only as accurate as the definitions, joins and verified questions they're given; the vendors' own numbers show it, with Databricks reporting 84.5% against 52.4% and Snowflake about twice the accuracy of a plain model once that layer exists. Most warehouses can't supply it because nobody has written down what each table means in machine-usable form. The pilot I'd run is one subject area, about 50 tables, 4 to 6 weeks: a readiness heatmap, owner work lists, a semantic layer for the top 10 to 15 tables, and 50 verified questions asked against raw tables and then with the layer. That before-and-after accuracy is the deciding number. I'd export through the Open Semantic Interchange where supported, so the layer isn't locked to one platform.

cards.title: Can AI write our missing metadata?
questions: can ai write the missing metadata for our tables

cards.answer: Yes as drafts, never as fact. In my framework AI does two jobs: it extracts rules hidden in prose descriptions into structured fields, and it drafts descriptions for undocumented tables from names, types, comments and lookups. Every draft is labeled AI-inferred, unconfirmed, carries a confidence note, goes to the owner's work list, and changes no score until a person confirms it. The research backs that split: grounded drafts were accepted by data stewards 87 to 88% of the time as is or with minor edits, while fully automatic descriptions recovered only about a third of the text-to-SQL gain human-written ones gave. What the model sees depends on the privacy tier: sample rows for open code tables, profile statistics for internal ones, metadata only for restricted tables, on owned hardware with open-weight models.

a client has budget for one ai project this year and three candidates: contract review, a customer service bot and demand forecasting. how would you help them choose, and what information would you ne
cards.answer: Two gates first: real business impact and data that's ready. If either fails, the project doesn't start. After that I rank by value and cost of adoption, not technical interest. On the legislative platform I sequenced the roadmap that way: one intake mailbox covers two of the three most-cited stakeholder pain points, and the only behavior change it asks is adding an address to a CC line. For Sponsored Programs, I prepared a ranked portfolio of nine AI agents across the proposal-to-cash lifecycle, with governance rules: human review, deterministic financial calculations and field-level provenance. I also separate problems that get blurred together, like a payables FAQ chatbot and a procurement price-comparison tool, so effort goes to the right one. And I flag schema decisions that are free now and expensive to retrofit later.

cards.answer: Adopt what's mature, build only the gap, and keep whatever compounds in-house. On the archival pipeline I directed a rubric-scored evaluation of Siegfried, DROID, BitCurator, ExifTool, Apache Tika, Docling, the NSRL set, ePADD, Preservica and Archivematica, with the deliverable being what to adopt, what to skip and what still needed writing. The integration rule: professional tools plug into the pipeline so their updates arrive free, and where the University already holds a license we use it. The readiness research split the same way: data quality monitoring and OpenMetadata coverage metrics are mature, so adopt; the readiness ladder, owner work lists and local-model enrichment don't exist, so build. On the legislative platform, bill data is a commodity any vendor sells, but a model of the institution's own interpretive stance can't be bought.

cards.title: Archival images: vendor moderation API, fine-tuning, or tuning what we have?
questions: would you use a vendor vision api or fine tune a model for archival images

cards.answer: I laid it out as a ladder by investment. Cheapest: tune the similarity threshold between 0.35 and 0.55 on a labeled validation set, since semantic similarity already beat LLaVA on historically contextual imagery and LLaVA added latency without accuracy gains. Middle: Google Vision SafeSearch, AWS Rekognition or Azure Content Moderator, the fastest path to reliable nudity and violence detection, with cost and procurement as the constraints. Top: fine-tune LLaVA on labeled University images for domain-specific content such as historical racialized performance and Indigenous cultural materials; most accurate long term, but it needs a labeled training set first. Two things narrowed it later. The production program's privacy position excludes hosted AI services, and 73% of flagged images were ambiguous, so a written appraisal policy and a gold set come before any training.

cards.answer: I build it around a break-even threshold and then try to break it. For the Research Funding platform, 480 AITS hours at $47 an hour came to about $22,560 against a sponsored research base of roughly $1.5 billion a year, so 1x recovery needed a funding uplift of 0.0015%. I checked it against half the adoption, double the hours and a smaller base, and the threshold still sat comfortably below any plausible outcome. Later I re-scoped it to 237 hours across eight roles, under the 250-hour work-request threshold, by reusing the production ingestion pipeline, existing NLP outputs and the validated on-prem inference pattern, without cutting functionality. The workforce case used labor benchmarks: turnover at 50 to 60% of salary, about $269 per vacant workday, giving $155K to $169K a year in benefits, labeled as benchmarks, not guaranteed savings.

cards.title: Making a savings estimate defensible
questions: how do you make a savings estimate defensible

cards.answer: Compute it from the most defensible matches, in code, normalized per unit. In procurement I matched 42,052 products as identical across four distributors on exact manufacturer plus part number, which is the tier I'd build a business case on. The raw spread looked like $317,583 in savings. Then I found the platform's qsu field, quantity sold as, populated on 6,068,599 of 6,068,888 rows; dividing price by qsu gave true unit prices and removed $156,019, 49.1% of the figure, as pack-size inflation. That left $161,564, which I present as the floor, not the ceiling. The model never does the arithmetic: the LLM's one job is equivalence judgment, returned as JSON, and savings are calculated deterministically in code. The next lever is data, not modeling: prior-year purchase quantities from the two catalog-only distributors could multiply the confirmed figure.

cards.answer: I split by workload shape. On the legislative platform, heavy batch inference runs on institution-owned GPU hardware at no marginal cost, and managed Azure OpenAI with gpt-4o-mini handles low-latency in-app requests, with results cached per bill and prompt so each pair is scored once. For the web tier I wrote a cost and scaling analysis of Basic against Premium v3: the app has a memory-bound ML startup profile, and on Basic it showed a crash loop, semantic search failing under memory pressure and cold-start cache loss, so I recommended the upgrade with the cost laid out. For procurement, the designed production path is App Service B3, the 8 GB floor for the FAISS index, plus Blob Storage and gpt-4o-mini, estimated at about $77 a month. What I haven't measured: GPU purchase cost against a hosted service, and I say so in the document evaluation.

cards.answer: Measure first, and check the serving layer before the card. Our server has one L4 with 23 GB of VRAM and 62 GB of RAM: 7B to 14B models run at full speed, 20B to 30B models fit quantized, and 70B-class is out. I took the position that hardware shouldn't be requested on principle; candidates that fit run a roughly 500-bill test first, since a well-prompted 14B with a strong parser often beats a poorly controlled 70B. The upgrade paths were a second L4, an A100 80GB only if 14B to 30B prove insufficient, or on-demand cloud GPU. The archival images showed why: under Ollama throughput sat flat near 9 images a minute with the GPU at 28 to 31%, so a faster card would have recovered nothing. vLLM on the same L4 reached 55.4 images a minute, a 6.22x speedup.

cards.answer: I write the decision rule before the run: the primary measure, the minimum useful improvement, the interval method, and what a pass earns. The interval's lower bound has to clear the minimum, and a screening win earns a confirmation on fresh cases, not adoption. In the document intelligence evaluation, vote3 was pre-registered as the single confirmatory method before the held-out run, and failed or truncated answers stayed in the denominator as zero. Results came from two machines, so I wrote a conformance contract: SHA-256 fingerprints of the frozen case manifests, every request, the client settings and the scorers, and a merge tool that refuses any export that fails. 40,975 scored rows merged. The outcome was routing per task for the prototype, explicitly not production approval.

cards.title: Prompting, retrieval or fine-tuning: which lever first?
questions: when should we fine tune a model

cards.answer: Cheapest lever first. Fix the instructions and checks, including contradictions between rules; switch or route models when a candidate passes a pre-registered rule and its confirmation; add retrieval or tools when the gap is missing or changing knowledge; fine-tune only when the best prompt and model still miss the bar and you can produce enough representative examples. In one screen a prompt review found a rule banning the phrase each other while another rule required it, and every model was tested under that conflict. LoRA or QLoRA can make some 27B runs feasible on a 32 GB card, but measure it. The main risk is a model that learns the checks instead of the job, so split before training, hold out cases, and run a regression suite on what the checks can't see.

cards.answer: I ask what in the task actually needs interpretation. Same-shape input and output is a workflow or plain code; ambiguous judgment on fuzzy inputs may need a model. Then I put the model last and narrow. In procurement the instinct is to hand the data to an assistant and ask it to find savings. That fails, because the data quality problem comes first. The design was exact manufacturer and part-number match in under 2 ms, then bge-small embeddings and FAISS narrowing 6 million rows to about 44 candidates in 75 to 110 ms, then qwen2.5:7b judging equivalence on that short list. For an archival appraisal agent, I put agentic loops at folder and collection level, not per file, since an agent loop costs many calls where a classification costs one: hours versus weeks at corpus scale.

My first accessible chart descriptions used AI; I rebuilt them so every description is calculated by rules from the chart's own data, because AI still gets chart facts wrong, about 1 in 5 numbers in one 2026 study. On the archival pipeline, facts already in a file header are phrased by a model, never discovered by one. In the retirement model I retired the unemployment, DJI and NASDAQ features on structure alone: they vary by time but not by person, so they can't change anyone's rank in a ranking report, and with 21 annual anchors the model can dress a year effect up as a market effect. And about 5% of bills were amendment-heavy outliers over 100,000 tokens; the fix was preprocessing them to the latest changes.

cards.answer: A risk register, a data inventory and controls that live in code. My governance proposals cover resource constraints, long-term support, adoption, LLM output quality, privacy and security, vendor concerns and accessibility, each with a mitigation tied to existing resources. The master data inventory classifies every source by sensitivity, documents every field the AI layer reads, and states the data boundary. On the archival pipeline the position is enforced in code: sensitivity outranks ranking, nothing is deleted, exclusion is a manifest decision, and machine proposals are distinguished from human judgments in an append-only log. On the legislative platform I designed around a specific risk: an AI misstating a named colleague's position inside a FOIA-able system, so users can correct their own characterization before others see it.

cards.answer: Treat them as decision support with layered review, and never let a ranking pose as a probability. Hiring, firing and anything affecting someone's livelihood keep a human accountable. The workforce plan put a fairness check across demographic groups before any individual-level output could be used, with interpretable heuristic fallbacks. On the retirement report, the column labeled probability had never been one: the top bin predicted 42.5% where 5.6% retired. I replaced it with two observed-rate bands, Elevated at 6.3% and Lower at 0.4%, with cut points frozen on earlier years and tested on later ones; a three-band version collapsed prospectively. The output may not be called projected retirements, and whether to rank resemblance or forecast departures is the business's policy choice.

cards.answer: Write the data boundary first, then design so the model never sees more than its tier allows. For the Research Funding platform the boundary statement said no new source queries, no extended access, and no document content leaving the on-prem environment for inference. My readiness framework tiers what a model sees: sample rows for open tables, profile statistics for internal ones, metadata only for restricted tables like medical or financial aid, nothing for excluded ones. The image taxonomy maps each category to its basis: FERPA for student records, HIPAA for health records, NAGPRA for human remains. For email, Presidio replaces entities with typed placeholders before a local model summarizes. Local processing is an architectural option; access control, encryption, logging and retention still have to be implemented and verified.

cards.answer: Set the bar before the run, then report against it. For document intelligence the acceptance target for numbers was 99% recall. Every model recovered 96.5% of the numbers in prose crops, and the best table route reached 97.4%, so numeric extraction is review-assisted, not unattended, and the first round recorded that no model or pipeline passed promotion. A small model matching a large one was published next to that gap. Layout masking raised word F1 from 0.814 to 0.881 but cut numeric recall from 0.872 to 0.694, so it stayed experimental. Institutional readiness is gated on a human-labeled set of about 100 documents, 20 double-labeled. For users, I state accuracy as decisions: the bill model is right on about 75% of the bills it flags.

cards.answer: Measure value in use, defined before the build. For bill prediction, AUC wasn't the KPI; I built a validation method around the precision of each call and the days of warning before the floor vote, with safeguards against counting predictions made after the outcome was known. On the held-out 103rd General Assembly that's 75.1% precision and 76.2% recall at a 0.70 threshold, median 21 days' warning. For the Research Funding platform, success meant sponsor approval of the feature schema, validated samples before full-corpus processing, and repeatable scheduled processing after launch. For data readiness, it's verified-question accuracy before and after the semantic layer. On the retirement report I report precision and recall at every candidate threshold, because flag volume is a policy choice.

cards.answer: By phase and role for people, from measured rates for compute, with assumptions marked provisional. The Research Funding plan had hours per activity across four phases, 80, 160, 140 and 100, for 480 hours over three months; the re-scope was 237 hours over about ten weeks, 138 of them development. For compute I time a real sample: the email pipeline measured 347.80 seconds per 10 rows, which projects to about 966 hours for 100,000 messages. I traced the cause, Ollama CLI reloading the model on every call, and listed options with estimates: persistent serving 5 to 10x, parallelism 4 to 8x, cloud APIs 100x or more. cards.answer: Lock the schema with the stakeholder before the build, and never pay for inference to reproduce a column that exists. For the Research Funding platform, every candidate feature was marked already structured, unknown, or not, and whether the LLM should extract it, yes, no or hybrid. Sponsor mapping was deterministic with LLM-assisted matching only for the long tail. On taxonomy I gave three options, anchor on HERDS, an independent LLM taxonomy, or a hybrid, and recommended the hybrid: HERDS as the broad anchor already classifying proposals, LLM themes as finer leaves, reconciled with sentence embeddings. LLM outputs were designed into sibling tables joined on FILE_DATA_ID, with model and prompt version per row. I also put ten candidate data sources on the table at design time, since adding them later costs more.

cards.answer: It's a model evaluation case study from October 2026 called Document Intelligence on One GPU: Which Local Model Reads What. I measured eleven open-weight models across seven tasks (prose OCR, tables, chart questions, chart to table, whole-page text, layout and contract clauses) under a frozen protocol, then confirmed the winners on data no model had seen. The result is 40,975 scored rows for rounds 1 and 2, with no scores given by a model judge. The deployment target is a single NVIDIA L4 or L40S, and I used public benchmarks only.

cards.answer: The most useful facts in proposals, contracts, awards and reports sit in scanned text, budget tables, charts, spreadsheets flattened into PDF and clauses on page forty. A database can't read them and neither can a search box. Each kind of extraction fails differently, so one accuracy number hides the one that matters. I defined solved as three things: the numbers are right, the source page is attached, and the system says so when it is unsure or couldn't read a page. Fluent text that is 90% right is a liability in a budget. Many of these documents also can't leave the organization.

cards.answer: Each kind of hard-to-reach information became one frozen task with its own public answer key and metric. Prose crop OCR used 50 OmniDocBench cases scored by character error rate and numeric recall. Table transcription used OmniDocBench and FinTabNet.c with 60 cases, scored by TEDS tree similarity and cell F1. Chart questions used 200 ChartQA cases with relaxed accuracy at 5% tolerance. Chart to table used 60 cases, whole-page text 40 scored by word F1, layout detection 120 at IoU 0.5, and clause extraction 24 cases from CUAD and ContractNLI, with 60 fresh documents on top. Tables, chart questions and pages also had held-out or fresh sets.

cards.answer: The desktop and laptop ran weeks apart under different runtimes, so I checked sameness in code. A conformance check fingerprints the frozen case manifests, the exact requests, the model-call settings and the scorers, and the merge tool refuses rows that fail. Cases were hashed before any model saw them, and held-out sets (2,181 cases in round 1, 1,988 in round 2) were used once. Every model got the same prompt, schema, token budget (300 to 6,000 by task) and image cap, at temperature 0. A thinking build burned its budget on hidden reasoning, so I removed it and deleted its rows. Qwen2.5-VL 7B reproduced in 11 of 13 comparison groups.

cards.answer: The final round tested four models never run before: three small parsers and gpt-oss-20b. I wrote the two leads down as hypotheses, then tested them on 100 FinTabNet.c tables and 80 unused OmniDocBench pages, all at an 8,192-token output budget against Qwen3-VL 32B AWQ. A hypothesis passed only if its main metric improved and numeric recall was no more than 0.02 worse, under a source-clustered bootstrap with Holm correction. PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 passed. cards.answer: Early legal runs showed models quoting text that wasn't in the cited span, or paraphrasing it enough to fail a string check. The fix takes copying out of the model's hands. Documents are split into blocks with IDs, retrieval supplies candidates, and the model returns only IDs and the label. My code copies the exact text, verifies its hash and location, and records absent fields explicitly. That removed every copy failure from the quoting design, 0 failed requests against 2 to 4 for the baseline. It doesn't prove the answer is right, and retrieval is the bottleneck: if the right block isn't a candidate, no design recovers it.

cards.title: Nemotron reassessment: a bad score is a configuration

cards.answer: A hosted Nemotron 3 Nano 30B scored 1/12 on CUAD, far below the local Qwen models. The easy conclusion was weak model. The honest one was weak configuration, untested. I ran 192 requests across eight configurations on the same 24 cases, changing one mechanism at a time: budget, reasoning, sampling, label definitions, full-document context, evidence by ID and schema delivery. Budget alone changed nothing, and reasoning lifted CUAD from 1/12 to 4/12. A pre-specified contrast on 60 fresh documents confirmed it: CUAD 3/30 to 13/30, ContractNLI 5/30 to 12/30, at the cost of one truncation per task. That supports enabling reasoning. It doesn't show production adequacy or a serving defect.

cards.answer: On 60 fresh public documents with identical requests and a 16,000-token budget, Qwen3 32B with thinking off scored 14/30 on CUAD and 18/30 on ContractNLI; thinking on gave 15 and 16. gpt-oss-20b at low reasoning scored 15 and 14, and at high reasoning 11 and 4, because it got truncated. Nemotron with reasoning on scored 13 and 12. The CUAD set holds 15 absent fields, so answering absent every time scores 15/30, and no configuration beat that. At 30 questions a task, differences of a few documents are noise, so I don't claim a winner on CUAD.

cards.answer: The target is one NVIDIA L4 (24 GB) or L40S (48 GB), but every final-round model ran on one 32 GB RTX 5090. Fit comes from weight sizes: about 2 GB for PaddleOCR-VL-1.6, 1.3 GB for Nemotron 3.5 Parse, 13 GB for gpt-oss-20b and 20 GB for a 4-bit 32B model. Everything recommended fits an L40S; on an L4 a 32B is tight. On a packet of 20 pages and 20 tables, four requests at a time, Nemotron Parse did 140 cases a minute, PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 73, olmOCR-2 19 and Qwen3-VL 32B AWQ 9. Bandwidth is about 1.8, 0.86 and 0.3 TB/s for the desktop, L40S and L4, so speeds there will be lower.

cards.answer: It's prototype evidence, not production certification. I did not measure speed on an actual L4 or L40S, purchase cost, or any total cost against a hosted service. The ranking should transfer to the target cards; the absolute numbers won't. No model reached the 99% bar for unattended numeric extraction, and the best table route reached 97.4%. Public scores say which model to try first, but an organization's own documents need their own labelled, document-disjoint test. Fresh means unused in earlier runs, not proven absent from pretraining. A local pipeline is an architectural option, not a security certification, and I used NIST AI 600-1 as the risk framing.

cards.answer: Routing came straight from the measured results. Tables go to PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 single pass. Whole pages go to Nemotron 3.5 Parse single pass with numbers checked. Prose crops use Qwen3-VL 8B baseline. Chart questions use 8B with self-check off, or 7B with it on; chart to data uses 8B with self-check. Layout uses DocLayout-YOLO. cards.answer: Six steps, each with a done-when. First, an intake service on the routing: a queue, checkpoints, bounded retries and one model per task, done when every file in a packet is processed and resumable with page-level evidence. Second, finer clause blocks for evidence by ID, measured against the retrieval ceiling. Third, a reviewer screen with source-page navigation and persisted corrections. Fourth, domain validation with independent human labels, a double-labelled subset and a document-disjoint holdout. Fifth, field-bound numbers, scoring each number in its own field and cell. Sixth, adapter fine-tuning of Qwen3-VL 8B after error analysis, shown on held-out documents of the same types.

cards.title: Engineering takeaways from the evaluation
questions: what are the takeaways of the document intelligence evaluation
what did the document intelligence study teach her

tags: method is part of the model
cards.answer: Six lessons. Define the problem as extraction types, not OCR: six tasks with six metrics exposed a 43-point swing one accuracy number would have averaged away. The method is part of the model, since self-check helped 7B by 26.5 points and hurt 8B by 43.5. Keep failures in the denominator, which made the thinking-build collapse and the first Nemotron result visible. Report numbers beside text, because masking raised word F1 by 0.067 and cut numeric recall by 0.178. Separate provenance from correctness. And treat a bad score as a configuration until proven otherwise.

cards.answer: My husband has collected and resold trading cards, collectible toys and watches since he worked at a card shop at 12. For months he was glued to his phone trying to catch limited drops, and he kept losing them to bots. These releases sell out in minutes, and nobody can refresh a dozen stores at once while living their life. So I built Drop Radar over one weekend. The goal was simple: he stops watching his phone, trusts the system to tell him when something matters, and we get that time back together. It is a personal project, and he is its real user.

cards.answer: I'd design it the way the archival pipeline is built, where hosted AI services are excluded outright. First, map the network precisely, because "no internet" is usually narrower than that; ours blocked Hugging Face only, so model weights come in through a documented staging path and get pinned by digest so a moved tag can't change the model. Serve with vLLM on the customer's GPU for continuous batching, behind a backend router so either vLLM or Ollama can serve by config. Keep embeddings, the vector index, extracted text and originals inside the network. Order the pipeline so cheap deterministic filters run first and the model only sees what survives. Make every long job checkpoint and resume, and route alerts through whatever the host allows; on our server that's local sendmail, since SMTP is locked down. Then get written confirmation from the customer's privacy office that local open-weight processing is acceptable.

cards.answer: Read narrowly, write reversibly, verify inside the run. The research proposals pipeline does change detection with an anti-join between attachment IDs in the source Kuali tables and those already processed, so each run touches only new documents and "nothing new" exits cleanly as a success. It pulls BLOBs in batches of 20, converts them to PDF, tolerates null or unconvertible files as logged warnings, and keeps credentials in a YAML config, never in code. Before every write it prints rollback SQL with the exact IDs and timestamp filter; afterward it counts rows in the destination and raises if the count falls short. The warehouse for the retirement report required Oracle Native Network Encryption, which thin mode can't negotiate, so it runs python-oracledb in thick mode, documented for Windows and Linux. All SQL lives in version-controlled files, and historical reads are effective-dated, never the current row.

The archival ingest constructs the manifest from name, size, SHA-1, path and timestamps alone, so inventory, deduplication and structural filtering all run first, and it checkpoints so a reclaimed Colab session resumes instead of restarting. cards.answer: The daily job starts with a LegiScan hash check, one API call regardless of bill count, and downloads only the sessions whose hash changed. Then it parses the JSON bill files, labels the new actions, rescores changed bills, builds an active-bills snapshot and uploads the session parquets to Azure Blob before saving the new hash. Older CSVs came from bulk exports with 5-digit internal IDs, while the server parsed real 7-digit LegiScan bill IDs from JSON, so only about 8,820 of 50,501 bills joined, and those by numeric collision. cards.answer: Mid-build I found the analytics server could reach Blob Storage but not Cosmos DB: the Cosmos endpoint was terminated at the TLS level at the campus boundary. That meant the on-prem pipeline couldn't read user prompts or write scores. I re-architected the data path around it. A serverless function exports user profiles and impact prompts from Cosmos to Blob; the server scores them against the local Llama model on vLLM; results go back to Blob as a long-format parquet, one row per user, prompt and bill; and the web app reads them through a dedicated loader with per-user filtering and cached reads. I kept a cache-first live path in the app that scores one bill on demand and writes the same schema, so batch and on-demand results are interchangeable. The split became a deliberate property: heavy batch inference on owned GPU hardware, low-latency requests on managed cloud inference.

cards.answer: Three are worth describing. First, an outage: the startup command reinstalled dependencies on every container boot, the install failed, and the container died with exit code 127. Users saw a page that kept refreshing. I changed it to a launch-only command with dependencies baked into the Oryx build. Second, a reliability cluster: semantic search failing under memory pressure and cache loss on cold start. I traced those to a shared cause, loaded columns and sessions selectively, configured always-on and start-time limits, and wrote a tier analysis that moved the plan from Basic to Premium v3 for the platform's memory-bound startup. Third, after a Functions deploy, output that read like a code regression was really stale workers serving the previous code. The standing remedy is restart, wait for warm-up, then trigger, plus a one-glance test that the new code is genuinely live.

cards.answer: Sign-in is a magic link built end to end. The app accepts only university email domains, issues an HMAC-signed one-time token, stores it in Cosmos DB with a TTL so it expires on its own, and sends the link through Azure Communication Services from a verified sender domain. A successful sign-in creates a server-side session record with a configurable multi-day TTL. One gate governs every page, and sessions are restored from the URL so a login survives a page refresh or a container recycle, which matters on App Service. Early on there was also a legacy admin password for demos. I removed it entirely, so university magic-link sign-in is the only route in. The same managed email service delivers the digests, so one verified domain covers both.

cards.answer: Cosmos DB is the platform's user-data store: profiles, magic-link tokens, sessions, saved items (tracked bills, categories, impact prompts) and impact-scoring results, with partition keys designed per container and TTL policies so tokens and sessions expire without cleanup jobs. The live app and the nightly scorer share incremental-write patterns and one result schema. The nightly function rescores only bills whose content hash changed, so a quiet night costs almost nothing. The in-app path is cache-first: a bill and prompt pair is scored once, stored, and read instantly after that. Profiles feed the model directly, so I put explicit limits on profile and prompt length to keep user-written context from silently truncating the prompt, and documented why for users. Once the campus firewall cut the server off from Cosmos, batch results moved to Blob with the same shape.

cards.answer: One L4 with 23 GB of VRAM serves several concurrent workloads, so memory and the host itself are the things to watch. From August 24 to September 3, 2026, legislative extraction failed silently for 11 nights; the cause was a server kernel update that disabled the GPU driver. I documented the cause for the system administrators, protected the catch-up so no data would be skipped, and restored the nightly scoring job. In early September I freed roughly 15 GB of shared GPU memory by right-sizing the language model's allocation, so the archival pipeline could run on the same server. Earlier, Ollama's keep_alive policy had been holding about 6 GB and blocking vLLM's cache. When the shared JupyterHub went down from an out-of-memory failure, I restored it and moved heavy jobs off it so it wouldn't recur.

cards.answer: Heavy work runs on-prem, user-facing work runs in Azure, and Blob Storage is the seam. On the Linux server with the L4: ingestion, chunking, LLM feature extraction, standardization, embeddings and the FAISS index, plus a daily prediction job scheduled through JupyterHub Scheduler at 4 AM that rescores changed bills and uploads session parquets to Blob. In Azure: the Streamlit app on App Service, reading Blob with a one-hour cache TTL so the morning rescore is visible the same day; a Function App on the same plan for weekly digests and nightly impact scoring; Cosmos DB for user data; Communication Services for sign-in links and email; and Azure OpenAI gpt-4o-mini for on-demand briefings. Batch inference on owned hardware has no marginal cost, and managed cloud inference handles low-latency in-app requests. I designed, provisioned and operate all of it.

cards.answer: Production means the system tells the truth about itself, survives bad inputs, and can be run by someone other than me. Between the approved February 2026 beta and the production version delivered to IGPA on August 11, 2026, I replaced a shared admin password with magic-link sign-in, made extraction idempotent so a multi-night run can be killed and restarted without double-writing, and audited the pipeline's own monitoring. I did SQL forensics first, from server job-history snapshots and DEBUG logs that record executed SQL verbatim, because query text disappears soonest. cards.answer: I keep the customer-specific part thin, on top of contracts that carry over. Every scheduled pipeline on our server writes Parquet logs to one schema, with PIPELINE_START and PIPELINE_END sentinel rows sharing a run ID, so a new pipeline is monitorable from day one by adding one path to the monitor's config. Onboarding the quarterly retirement pipeline needed only a per-pipeline silence threshold of 2,400 hours, since the default 48-hour rule would alert for 89 days after every run. The legislative pipeline takes a multi-state config.json, so it is ready for California expansion, and its inference router switches serving stacks by flag. When the SPA research funding platform was re-scoped, reusing the existing ingestion pipeline, NLP outputs and on-prem inference pattern took it from a 480-hour proposal to a 237-hour work request without removing functionality.

cards.answer: For payroll the interface is a Box folder. The old CPA and PUA processing was manual and semi-manual in Excel. I rebuilt it as a Python transformation framework that applies the business-rule mappings, deduplication and derived fields, with Box for both source and destination: staff upload files and processing follows. File type is detected from the naming convention, so nobody configures which kind of file it is, which removes a whole class of operator error. cards.answer: The Library engineer's university-standard laptop has integrated graphics and no discrete GPU, which rules out local high-throughput serving and makes local multimodal inference impractical. So Colab's T4 is her primary compute, and her local plan is CPU-first: a small text model, a small vision model and local embeddings, called through the Ollama HTTP API. Not the CLI, because the CLI reloads model weights on every call, which is exactly what produced 34.8 seconds per row in the email proof of concept. Real archival content can't go to Google infrastructure, so I built her a validation kit with a synthetic corpus, scoring code, notebook, rubric and brief. The working rules are explicit: credentials in a secrets manager, never a notebook cell; outputs cleared before commit; jobs checkpointed to resume; and no accession content in any public repository.

cards.answer: I enforce the boundary mechanically, because a promise doesn't survive a busy week. On the archival build, hosted AI services are excluded: models, embeddings, extracted text, the vector index and the originals stay inside the institutional network, with written confirmation sought from Data Privacy and Governance. The public demonstration build is produced by a sanitizer that refuses to write if any identifying content survives. Before publishing the repository I caught a notebook with 377 MB of embedded outputs that would have put email content in public. For document intelligence, the rule is that AI coding assistants write and run code but see aggregate metrics only; local models do all reading, and a privacy gate script denies institutional identifiers before anything reaches GitHub. On the retirement pipeline, output pairs names with salary, so credentials live outside the repository and every extract is gitignored.

cards.answer: Secrets live in platform configuration or files outside the repository, never in code or notebooks. The legislative platform's secret surface spans Cosmos keys, Azure OpenAI keys, Communication Services connection strings and deployment credentials, all held in App Service and Function App configuration, with a rotation practice that uses secondary keys so a rotation causes no downtime. The research proposals pipeline loads database credentials through a YAML config loader. The retirement pipeline keeps them in a restricted environment file outside the repository, and its preflight verifies they load before the first scheduled run. Before sharing the prediction training code with outside collaborators, I removed an embedded API key, storage credentials and local file paths. For the Library's engineer the rule is written down: credentials go in a secrets manager, never a notebook cell.

cards.title: Designing for graceful degradation
questions: what if the model is down

partial availability design
cards.answer: Every AI component should be optional to the core path. In procurement, Tier 1 exact matching on manufacturer and part number always runs, under 2 ms, even when the LLM is offline; semantic candidates still display for manual review, so the system never returns nothing. In the legislative app, LLM briefings run on open-weights Llama through Groq and degrade cleanly when no API key is configured. The automated bill investigator is deliberately decoupled from the nightly scoring core, so a failure in deep-dive generation can't take down routine scoring, and its reader layer deploys independently. The monitoring side follows the same rule: an unreadable log file becomes a synthetic LOG_READ_FAILED record and an alert, instead of disappearing.

cards.answer: Size from the workload's real constraint, usually memory at startup for these apps, and give the decision-maker the cost trade-off in writing. The legislative app loads ML artifacts and data on start, so I evaluated Basic against Premium v3 for that memory-bound profile, wrote the cost and scaling analysis, and recommended the upgrade; it resolved the crash and cold-start cluster. cards.answer: I narrow the problem to a layer I can prove, then hand the owner of that layer evidence rather than a symptom. Three patterns recur. Network: on two occasions a destination failed at the TLS handshake while neighbors worked (Hugging Face but not GitHub or PyPI; Cosmos DB but not Blob), and testing each endpoint separately turned a vague "it can't connect" into a specific constraint I could design around or raise as an exception. Dependencies: the vLLM stand-up failed three ways at once, all version drift and VRAM contention rather than engine bugs, so I fixed them in order instead of patching code. Platform behavior: a deploy that looked like a code regression was stale workers serving old code. And the host itself: an 11-night silent failure traced to a kernel update disabling the GPU driver, documented for the system administrators.

cards.answer: It's an October 2026 case study where I screened seven local model configurations, covering six models, on the real generator behind my personal project Skyrule. The generator writes a plan, then a piece, and code checks both. Its yield had stalled at 3 of 20 groups. Under a decision rule frozen before the run, Qwen3.8 27B accepted 7 of 20, and a second pre-registered round on 60 new groups replicated it, 24 against 11. The public IFEval ranking disagreed with the task ranking. Qwen3.8 is eligible for the release route, not adopted, and nothing on the page is release validation.

cards.answer: A trial run on 20 frozen test groups finished within its bounds but kept only 3 of 20, against a pre-registered bar of 9. A separate measurement found every first plan failed at least one check, with a median of five failing checks per plan. The anchor words were present for all 20 groups, but one rule banned the phrase "each other" while every accepted wording of one goal contained it. So the low yield could come from the model, the serving setup, the instructions, or all three. The screen asked one narrower question: with prompt, checks and bar fixed, does another local configuration accept clearly more groups?

cards.answer: An arm earned a full trial if it accepted at least four more groups than the baseline and did not accept fewer on the first try. I wrote that before any model loaded and froze it by hash. I'm clear about its limits: the four-group margin is a screening threshold with no calibrated false-positive control across several candidates, and with seven arms on 20 groups one arm can clear it by luck. That's why passing only earned a full trial, not adoption. Fluent writing that fails a check counts as a rejected piece, so the generator's own checks were the score.

cards.answer: Incidents were recorded as they happened, and affected results were discarded or flagged. In the first IFEval window the bench's watcher saw an unexpected model load and stopped Gemma 4's run. I first attributed it to a morning check-in job; a later diagnosis traced it to an hourly agent round that falls back to a local model when the resident service is down. cards.answer: Several things. The checks are the score, not a measure of writing quality beyond what they test, and a model judge gave 0 scores. Twenty frozen groups and one seed say little about small differences or other groups, and round 2's 60 groups came from a single job. Each arm is a bundle of model, server, quantization, template and sampling, so I can't attribute a difference to any one of them. The best round 1 result, 7 of 20, was still below the bar of 9. Other task types weren't tested, and nothing here is release validation or a production decision.

cards.answer: Qwen3.8 is eligible for the release route, not adopted. Taking it into the generator is a release decision: its own canary run, an independent quality review and the project owner's approval of the model change. The next piece is a pre-registered fine-tuning experiment with its own build, which reserves the round 2 groups from training and validation data. Its first pilot stopped on a server setup error, recorded and fixed, and has been re-queued, so no fine-tuning result is reported. A wider model search remains possible later. cards.answer: I did the evaluation design, the orchestration and the failure analysis. The workload belongs to Skyrule, my self-funded personal project, and the bench ran on one RTX 5090 using Ollama and vLLM. My coordinating agent, Claude, unloaded an unexpected model by hand in the first IFEval window so the restore and results could proceed. The design went through two independent model-review rounds, and an independent audit of the write-up found overstatements that are now corrected on the page. It is an October 2026 case study of screening evidence, not a production decision.

cards.answer: Six things. Measure the task as well as the leaderboard, because the IFEval ranking and the task ranking differed. Check the harness and the instructions, since a reproduced baseline doesn't prove the prompts are sound and a review found a contradiction. Compare bundles and say so. Decide before you look, and keep the decision small, so a screening result doesn't become an adoption. A shared GPU needs isolation, not good timing. And have the write-up audited: the first draft had causal claims the data didn't support, a units error and figures from the wrong window. The corrected page says less and is more defensible.

cards.answer: I held the prompt, checks and bar fixed so any change in accepted groups could be attributed to the configuration, and I used the generator's own code checks as the score so there's no model judge and no scoring subjectivity: 0 scores came from a model. Rejected and timed-out groups stay in the denominator of 20, so a configuration can't look good by dropping hard cases. The screening rule was frozen by hash before running, on 20 frozen groups. Only counts and check names are reported, never generated text. In round 2 I tested the candidate prompt as a separate factor rather than changing it under the screen.

cards.answer: It's an advisory guide from October 2026 for teams choosing an open-weight model for a specific job. Model names are full of numbers like 8B, 27B, 35B-A3B, Q4 and AWQ that look like a ranking and aren't one, so the guide explains what the labels mean, how models are commonly trained, why a smaller model can beat a bigger one on a task, and a method for picking, validating and, only when needed, fine-tuning. It combines findings from my own generation screen and document intelligence evaluation with general engineering guidance. It was independently reviewed and revised after technical feedback.

cards.answer: Those numbers are not a ranking. 27B or 32B means roughly that many billion parameters, the numbers the model learned in training. It's a design choice that sets capacity, but it says nothing about how well the model was trained or how well it follows instructions. Version and release date identify a release, and its documentation may disclose training changes and data, yet neither size nor release date alone identifies the best model for a task. The guide treats size and release date as starting points, so the model still has to be tested on your own job.

cards.answer: 35B-A3B names a mixture of experts: roughly 35 billion parameters in total, about 3 billion active per token, depending on the vendor's counting convention. Sparse activation can reduce computation compared with a similar dense model, but actual speed depends on the hardware and the serving software, and all the weights still need storing, so memory isn't saved. Active parameter count is also not a quality score. In the guide I treat it as one fact about cost and capacity, to be confirmed by measuring the model on my own hardware and task.

cards.title: Quantisation formats Q4 and AWQ in the guide

cards.answer: Q4 and Q4_K_M are approximately 4-bit weight formats with some mixed precision and storage overhead. They shrink the weights so a large model fits on one card, but not every other use of memory, such as the context cache. AWQ is a quantisation method, not a bit width, so check the actual bit width of the checkpoint you download. Different methods lose different things, so the same model can behave differently under each. That's why the guide says to run the same model under each quantisation you're considering instead of assuming they match.

cards.title: Instruct, base and thinking models in the guide
questions: what is the difference between instruct and base models in the local model guide

cards.answer: Instruct and chat models are adapted to respond to requests, and they're usually the starting point for assistant-style applications. Base models are mainly pretrained continuation models and suit specialized adaptation. Thinking or reasoning models may generate intermediate reasoning tokens before the final answer. That can help hard problems, but whether you can see or switch off the reasoning depends on the model and the server, and it costs time and token budget. In the guide I list reasoning mode among the settings to record, because it changes both results and cost.

where does a model's knowledge and fluency come from
where do the preferences come from in model post-training
is the three-stage recipe universal for every model
cards.answer: The guide describes a common recipe in three stages, and says plainly it's not universal because vendors publish different amounts of detail. Pretraining is next-token prediction over very large amounts of text and code, often trillions of tokens, and it gives much of the knowledge and fluency. Supervised instruction tuning trains on requests paired with good responses, which turns a continuation model into an assistant. Preference optimization or reinforcement learning then pushes toward preferred responses, whether the preferences come from people, a reward model or automatic checks. Data, compute and all three stages matter alongside parameter count.

cards.answer: In my generation screen, Qwen3.8 27B accepted 7 of 20 test groups through a strict generator's checks, against 3 for the larger Qwen3-32B configuration it would replace, which met a pre-registered screening rule. A second pre-registered round on 60 new groups replicated it: 24 accepted against 11, a difference of 21.7 points with a 95% interval of 6.6 to 35.5. It's still a comparison of configurations, one on Ollama and one on vLLM, on one job's groups, and adopting it remains a release decision.

cards.title: The prompt conflict found in the generation screen
questions: can i trust the qwen3.8 numbers given the flawed prompt in the guide

cards.answer: A prompt review found that one rule banned the phrase "each other" while another required wording containing it. Every arm in the screen ran the same pinned prompt, the one with the conflict, copied from the release version and checked by hash. So the figures are pipeline outcomes under that prompt, not a clean measure of either model's general instruction-following. A corrected prompt has to be versioned and re-tested on both models before any adoption. I kept the finding in the guide because it limits what the numbers can claim.

cards.answer: At the first plan check, the smaller model's plans were flagged by the copying check in 2 groups against 7 and by the causal-leap check in 0 against 4. But the behaviour-only check, which also covers feelings, causes, outcomes and labels, flagged 9 against 0. Both models were flagged by the exact-anchor check in 15 groups. These are checker flags at the first plan, not counts across retries or a semantic audit. It shows the guide's point that a new model trades one set of failures for another, so only a confirmation run tells you whether the trade holds.

cards.answer: Newer post-training is one possible explanation, but the screen didn't separate it from architecture, quantisation, server, chat template or decoding differences, so it supports a configuration-level result, not a causal one. The guide gives general reasons a smaller model can win: a different or later training recipe can matter more than extra parameters, parameter count alone doesn't establish fit to a task's constraints, and quantisation, server and template change behavior. A model that fits fully on the card at the needed context also usually runs faster, which matters when a pipeline retries.

cards.answer: The guide cites it as evidence that a model name isn't the unit being tested: the same 32B accepted 3 groups under one backend configuration and 1 under another. Quantisation, server and chat template change behavior, so what I compared in the screen was configurations, one on Ollama and one on vLLM, not models in the abstract. That's why the method says to run the same model under each server and quantisation you're considering, with a control arm for each change, so you can attribute a difference to the thing you changed.

cards.title: What public benchmarks can and cannot tell you in the guide
