cards.answer: Use public benchmarks to build a shortlist, not as the verdict. In my screen, Gemma 4 had the highest IFEval score of the four models completed, 0.900 against the baseline's 0.830, and accepted 0 of 20 task groups: 3 exhausted their plan retries, 14 their writing retries, and the recorded refusal reasons show the other 3 stopped early after repeated failures. Qwen3.8 had the lowest, 0.806, and accepted the most. IFEval measures its own verifiable instructions, not every capability a pipeline needs, and public test material can leak into training data.

cards.title: Step one of the method: find candidates and check the licence
questions: how does the guide say to find candidate local models

cards.answer: Start from what fits your hardware at the context, output length and concurrency you need, including the context cache and runtime overhead. Then shortlist from benchmarks, recent releases and the families you already run. Check each release's licence, acceptable-use terms and commercial and redistribution rights, plus any obligations that come with adapters or training data, because open-weight does not mean unrestricted. Write down reliability requirements alongside speed, including how failures, timeouts and exhausted retries will be handled, and include your current model as the baseline.

cards.title: Step two: turn the real task into a test
questions: does the guide count timeouts as failures

cards.answer: Freeze a set of real cases with code-based checks or answer keys, and keep failed and timed-out answers in the denominator so a model can't look better by failing quietly. Then account end to end: input and output tokens, retries, runtime and cost per successful case, plus latency and throughput. If you need long inputs, test quality at that length instead of trusting the advertised context limit.

cards.title: Writing the decision rule before the run
questions: how does the guide decide in advance what a win is

cards.answer: State the primary measure and the direction of comparison, the minimum useful improvement, the interval method and confidence level, how candidates are selected, when you'll stop, and what a pass earns. Require the interval's lower bound, not just the estimate, to clear the minimum useful improvement, and count groups or cases, not retries, as the independent units. A rule written first reduces discretion but doesn't remove small-sample uncertainty or the chance that one of several candidates wins by luck, so use a pre-specified multiplicity procedure or an independent confirmation design, finishing candidate selection before looking at confirmation results.

cards.answer: Reproduce the baseline within a stated tolerance and investigate any mismatch. Separately, test the checks on known passing, failing and borderline examples, review the instructions for contradictions, and audit a sample by hand or with a validated grader. Reproducing the baseline alone doesn't prove the test is valid, because a harness can reproduce an old number and still have a broken checker. The prompt conflict in my own screen is a related example: a prompt review found two rules that contradicted each other.

cards.answer: Run the same model under each server and quantisation you're considering, and test prompt changes separately from model changes, so each difference has one cause. Record exact checkpoint and tokenizer revisions, chat template, server version, quantisation, reasoning mode, decoding settings, context and output budgets, stopping rules, retry policy and seeds. A shared seed doesn't guarantee identical runs, so I don't treat seeds as proof of reproducibility. The checklist asks the same thing: a control arm for each change and every setting recorded.

cards.title: Confirming a screening win on fresh cases
questions: does the guide rerun the winner on data it has not seen

cards.answer: A screening win earns a confirmation, not adoption. The confirmation uses cases not used in local training, prompt development or model selection, with a paired interval whose lower bound clears the minimum useful improvement. You can control what you used, but you usually can't prove what a vendor's model saw in training. My generation screen followed this: the 7 of 20 versus 3 screening result was followed by a second pre-registered round on 60 new groups, 24 accepted against 11, with a 95% interval of 6.6 to 35.5 on the difference.

cards.title: The order of levers before fine-tuning
questions: in what order does the guide say to try levers before fine-tuning
why does fine-tuning come last in the local model guide
what should you fix before fine-tuning a model

cards.answer: The order is: fix the instructions and checks, switch or route models, add retrieval or tools, and only then fine-tune. Fixing instructions is low effort and always first, because the guide says to look for contradictions between rules. Switching or routing needs evaluation time, and fits once a candidate meets your pre-registered rule and its confirmation; a different model per stage can help when failures differ by stage. Retrieval or tools fit when the problem is missing or changing knowledge, not behavior. Fine-tuning needs data, training and validation, so it's for when the best prompt and model still miss your bar and you can produce enough good, representative examples.

cards.title: Rejection-sampling fine-tuning and preference tuning
questions: what is rejection-sampling fine-tuning in the local model guide
how do automatic checks supply cheap labels for fine-tuning
what should you audit when fine-tuning on outputs that pass checks

how do you build preference pairs for the same request
cards.answer: With rejection-sampling fine-tuning, automatic checks provide cheap labels for the properties they actually test. After validating the checks, you sample many outputs, keep those that pass and also meet your quality requirements, and fine-tune on them, auditing coverage, diversity and signs of the model exploiting the checks. A better first-try pass rate is a hypothesis to test on held-out cases, not a guarantee. Preference tuning pairs a preferred and a rejected response for the same request, and the preference has to reflect the quality you want, not length or style. Methods such as DPO or reward-model reinforcement learning can learn from the pairs, but noisy preferences teach the wrong lesson.

cards.title: LoRA and QLoRA on one GPU

cards.answer: LoRA trains small low-rank adapter weights while the base model usually stays frozen; how many weights that is depends on the rank and which layers are adapted. QLoRA does the same over a frozen low-bit copy of the base. That can make some 27B training runs feasible on a 32 GB card, but the guide is careful: feasibility must be measured for your sequence length, batch size and software. Keep the exact base checkpoint and the adapter's configuration together with the adapter, since the adapter is only meaningful against that base.

cards.title: How to validate a tuned model
questions: how does the guide check a tuned model did not regress on general skills

cards.answer: Split before you train, as whole cases, and de-duplicate at whatever level prevents leakage between related cases, documents or templates. Use validation data for tuning decisions and keep the test set untouched until the decision point. Run tuned and untuned models on the same base checkpoint, server, quantisation, prompt and settings, and record any differences you can't remove. Guard what the checks can't see with a small regression suite and a pre-specified quality review, with a rubric, stated sample size and sampling procedure, blinded where feasible, with limits stated in advance and subgroup and stage-level failures reported, not just the average.

cards.answer: A failed test of one recipe doesn't show that fine-tuning cannot help; it shows that this data, recipe and setup did not clear the bar. A tuned model that does pass still goes through the normal release route: a small live trial, a quality review and a way back. As for status, a fine-tuning experiment following this method is designed for the generation screen, and its results will be added when it finishes. So the guide's fine-tuning sections are method, not reported results, and run results are specific to the configurations and cases tested.

cards.title: The one-page model selection checklist

cards.answer: It's ten questions, each with a good answer. Does the model fit at my context, output length and concurrency, measured on my hardware including cache? Is the licence checked for the exact release? Is the test my real task with validated checks? Did I fix what better means first, in a written rule frozen before the run? Does the current model reproduce its known result? Are server, quantisation, prompt and model separated? Did the winner hold on fresh cases? Did I fix instructions and try other models before fine-tuning? Is the test set kept apart? Did general skill and quality hold within limits stated in advance?

cards.title: How did you go from data engineer to leading AI work?
questions: how did you go from data engineer to leading ai work
tell me about your career path

cards.answer: I joined the Advanced Analytics team in May 2022 as a Data Engineer, working mostly in KNIME with Python and SQL alongside it. cards.title: What is Agent City?

cards.answer: I run about 30 AI agents on my own machine as a hobby. They clear my inbox, write news reports, do personal research and keep my knowledge bases up to date, each with a specific job across my side projects. As they got more done, following everything through chats and logs got exhausting, so I built a 3D world to visualize and interact with the system. I call it Agent City; it's a working title. Each agent has its own office, and the town is built around places I love: Geisel Library at UCSD, a Topanga Canyon retreat, Downtown Cary Park with a treehouse, and a jazz kissaten cafe with Spotify hooked up and a mushroom agent behind the counter who suggests records. I can walk into a building, sit down with an agent and talk through its work, or hold a board meeting with the agents I choose. The town shows me completed tasks, recent decisions, bottlenecks and what needs my input. It feels a little like a Black Mirror episode, but honestly it brings me real joy. It's the modern version of decorating my cubicle, except it's a whole world that's functional and feels like me.

cards.answer: Each agent has a defined role, its own niche domain knowledge, responsibilities, history and persistent memory. A program manager, a principal architect and a founder agent coordinate the work and make decisions between the others. They hand tasks between departments, and file ownership is enforced, so an agent can only change what it owns. Decisions go into shared records, and a job queue manages schedules, dependencies, retries and approval gates. I can swap an agent's "brain" for the task: a stronger cloud model like Claude for demanding work, or one of about 20 models stored locally to save tokens. I decide when it's worth spending money. I set direction and make the decisions that need me. The agents coordinate the routine work and run overnight, with quality and security checks built in.

cards.title: What do you think of running AI across cheap consumer devices?
questions: what do you think of running ai across cheap consumer devices
can you run big ai models on small devices
what's the future of local ai
will ai end up in everyday devices
cards.answer: What I find most interesting is treating consumer hardware as a distributed inference cluster instead of just buying a bigger GPU. Seeing a 70B model run across a few Raspberry Pis and Mac minis completely changed how I think about local AI. I can imagine affordable AI built into toys, cameras, home assistants and everyday appliances, all powered by a small fabric of inexpensive devices working together. The model doesn't care if the hardware looks pretty; it just needs the work to get done.

cards.title: Will the best AI models stay affordable?

is there an ai bubble
what happens when ai gets expensive
do you think open models will win
cards.answer: I share the concern. Even when model weights are free to download, the hardware to run them can still be far out of reach. My hope is that "highly capable" won't always mean huge and expensive. Distillation, better training and more efficient designs give us reasons to keep pushing for more intelligence with less compute. I'd love smaller models to become something we choose because they do the job well, not just because we've been priced out of everything else.

cards.title: What's the downside of relying on hosted AI APIs?
questions: what's the downside of relying on hosted ai apis
why do you run models locally
is it safe to send your data to ai companies
cloud ai or local ai
cards.answer: Privacy is a big part of it, but it's also about control: over pricing and over whether a model stays available. Hosted APIs are genuinely useful. I just like running models independently when I can, because having the model and your data on your own hardware gives you more control over what you share and with whom. The catch is that getting there with large models takes a lot of money upfront, plus time and technical commitment. For startups, independent founders and research labs that independence often isn't affordable, and that gap matters when we talk about AI being accessible to everyone.

cards.title: What does idempotent mean?
questions: what does idempotent mean
what is idempotency
why do retries need to be safe
cards.answer: Breaking down the word itself: "idem" is Latin for "the same", and "potent" comes from the Latin for "power" or "ability". So idempotent means, roughly, "having the same effect": doing something again has no additional effect after the first time. In a pipeline, that means a retry can't create duplicate records or payments.

cards.title: What's your take on saving money and early retirement?

what do you think about the fire movement
should i skip the latte to retire early

cards.answer: It's not about how much you save, it's about financial leverage. Money is a tool, not an asset, unless you're doing something with it. The goal is to turn money into more income: investments, career growth, creating jobs or businesses, anything that creates value beyond just saving. That's where real freedom comes from. If you save 97% of a small paycheck by eating lentils in a basement, and I save the same share of a bigger paycheck and still buy the latte, neither of us has escaped the system. Different sized cages, both still prisons. Mine just has coffee.

cards.title: Are open-weight models really accessible?
questions: are open-weight models really accessible
what do you think about open-source ai models
can you run big open models at home
why does model size matter
cards.answer: Free to download doesn't mean affordable to run. The biggest open models can write and debug software and reason through complex tasks, but running them yourself takes multiple high-end machines or enterprise GPUs. For perspective, renting eight H200 GPUs at about $5.29 per GPU-hour comes to roughly $30,000 a month if you leave them running. That's an illustration, not a quote. Cloud rentals and hosted APIs help, and APIs can be much cheaper for individuals, but then you depend on another company to run the model for you. So the accessibility conversation needs to go further. I want highly capable models that run on hardware people can realistically own. The next goal should be getting more intelligence out of less computing power.

Building Agent City, personalizing it and making it feel like a game means checking in on my projects is something I genuinely look forward to.

cards.title: Is AI a threat to software companies?

cards.answer: I think all SaaS faces a very real risk of being replicated, with competitors independently rewriting software to offer the same functionality. The biggest advantages established companies will keep are the data no one else has and the capital to access better resources. But as engineers start rebuilding existing software and selling it for less or making it open source, the big players will have to compete with products that are just as good at a fraction of the cost, built with minimal overhead. I feel like this could snowball very quickly.

cards.title: How do you know the bill passage model isn't too good to be true?
questions: how do you know the bill passage model isn't too good to be true
how accurate is the bill passage model
how did you validate the legislative model
how do you prevent data leakage
cards.answer: A model this accurate at predicting passage should make you suspicious, because procedural history leaks the answer. So I apply the leakage guard at a single point before aggregation, split at bill level rather than row level, and keep the raw labeled history as an audit artifact so the guard can be inspected rather than trusted. That suspicion paid off. In September 2026 I traced gaps in the training corpus to a status filter: passed bills were almost missing, and resolutions were pooled with bills, inflating the success rate to 30.4% from a true 13.2%. I rebuilt the corpus from 46,815 to 117,722 bills and retrained on the corrected definitions. The honest numbers are the ones I publish now: on a held-out General Assembly, 75.1% precision and 76.2% recall at a 0.70 threshold, with a median of 21 days' warning before the floor vote. Adding each bill's title and synopsis lifted introduction-time ROC-AUC from 0.561 to 0.845, confirmed by an ablation study and three leakage checks. Catching your own inflated numbers is the job.

cards.title: How did you build Drop Radar in a weekend?

A dedicated Claude Code agent owns the system, with written rules and a living knowledge file, and a job queue runs its daily and weekly reviews while I sleep. Under the hood it's plain Python: store feeds, waiting-room detection, page and RSS watchers, a Telegram bot, Discord's official live connection, a dashboard on GitHub Pages, and an email-reading ledger. When I wanted a second opinion on strategy, I ran it past ChatGPT and took its best free ideas the same day.

cards.answer: The collector community lives on Discord, so I joined my husband to nine of the best free restock servers and wired their alert channels into his own private server, where Drop Radar's bot reads them over Discord's official live connection. Posts arrive in about a second. Then it filters hard: online only, retail price only, from the real store. No resellers, no marked-up third-party listings, and no "spotted at a store three states away."

cards.title: How does Drop Radar track purchases and sales?

Every order confirmation, shipping notice and eBay sale lands there, and the system reads it automatically: what he bought, when, what he paid, whether it shipped, and what it's worth now. It works out his eBay profit after fees, reminds him before a ship-by deadline, and suggests what to sell and what to hold. All of it stays on our home computer, never on the public website.

cards.title: What did you learn building Drop Radar?

cards.answer: That the person using the thing is the real product manager. His first verdict on my early alerts was brutal and fair, and every big improvement came from his feedback, which is why the weekly check-in is built in. And that the best tech gives people time back. Success isn't more notifications. It's my husband putting his phone down because he trusts it'll tell him when something matters.

cards.answer: I looked into it properly. Every major store bans checkout bots in its terms and quietly runs bot detection, and some cancel bot orders outright. I didn't want to put his accounts or his orders at risk. So Drop Radar does the part a person can't: it watches everything, all the time, and gets him there in time. Where a store allows it, the alert even opens checkout with the item already in his cart. He still taps Buy himself.

cards.title: How does Drop Radar improve itself?

cards.answer: This is my favorite part. The Telegram bot isn't just an alert channel, it's a two-way line to an AI agent. My husband can text it, send a voice note or a screenshot: "watch this brand," "that alert was junk," "this came in too late." The agent reads it, works out the fix, rewrites its own code or adds new sources, tests it, and replies with what it changed. He never touches a line of code. And once a week it checks in on its own, asking what's working and what isn't, so the people using it are the ones steering it.

cards.title: What is Drop Radar?

cards.answer: Drop Radar is the alert system I built for my husband in a weekend. He's a lifelong collector: he worked at a card shop when he was 12, and even with a completely different career he's always loved collecting and reselling. For months he was glued to his phone hunting drops and losing every one to bots, because limited items sell out in minutes. He's on his phone way less now, and we get our evenings back.

cards.answer: Within days! It found a limited-edition watch, only 100 made, that sold out in minutes, and my husband got one. The funny part is that none of the scripted trackers caught it. The AI deep search did, by hunting the web for small-batch limited editions. That taught me something: for the rarest drops, an AI that goes looking beats a feed that waits.

cards.title: How did you handle 79,000 legacy emails?

cards.answer: The email pipeline processed more than 79,000 legacy .eml files: recursive ingestion with metadata extraction, regex header parsing, fuzzy-matched sender analysis, and LDA topic modeling with topic labels generated by LLaMA. To protect people's information I used Presidio to detect more than ten kinds of personal data, with five anonymization strategies covering substitution, redaction, masking and hashing, and the summaries the LLM writes are made from de-identified text.

cards.title: Did economic factors help predict enrollment?

cards.answer: I tested external economic and demographic factors as extra inputs to the ARIMA enrollment forecasts. The correlations were weak. That was still a useful result: it told leadership something real about how little those outside forces were moving enrollment trends, which shaped their decisions.

cards.title: How does the Legislative Insights platform work for its users?
questions: how does the legislative insights platform work for its users
how does the legislative app personalize results
how do users log in to the legislative platform
what's the architecture of the legislative app
cards.answer: It's a multi-tab Azure app that gives University leadership a working view of state legislation affecting the institution. The proof of concept was approved in February 2026, and I delivered it to the Institute of Government and Public Affairs as a production platform in August 2026. Sign-in is passwordless: magic links with HMAC-signed tokens that expire, and sessions that survive container recycles. It uses Azure Functions, Cosmos DB and Communication Services, with inference split between Azure OpenAI and on-prem vLLM. It was the first multi-service cloud AI deployment in my team's history. Each stakeholder defines their own analytical lens, applied across the full active-bill corpus, so the same bill reaches a budget analyst and an AI-ethics researcher framed differently.

cards.title: What production problems did you hit deploying to Azure?

what's the hardest bug you've debugged

cards.answer: Two stand out. A startup command was getting the container killed by a health-check timeout, so the app looked like it was crashing when it was really just starting too slowly. The other was a campus firewall terminating the Cosmos DB connection at the TLS layer. That one meant re-architecting scoring into a hybrid split rather than fighting the network.

cards.title: What kinds of failures does your monitoring system catch?
questions: what kinds of failures does your monitoring system catch
how do you detect silent pipeline failures
how do you avoid alert fatigue
cards.answer: It catches script failures, upstream cascade failures, missing or skipped runs, failures that only show up after server downtime, and silent pipelines, which it spots with start and end marker rows each job writes. Alerts are tiered by severity: critical if it happened within 24 hours, warning within 7 days, and info for anything older or caused upstream. That keeps alert fatigue down without losing the diagnostic detail, and each email includes the error type, traceback, run ID, stage name and timestamp.

cards.title: How do you run a project across two organizations?

how do you manage projects
how do you track dependencies
do you do project management as well as engineering
cards.answer: I built and run the work breakdown, the milestone plan and a project board shared by both organizations. Every issue has an owner, its dependencies, explicit acceptance criteria and a link to the design section it implements. Blocked is a column rather than a label. That keeps the cross-organizational dependencies visible, things like appraisal policy, service account authorization and where the PII mapping store lives, so nobody can quietly lose track of them.

cards.title: How are you handing the archival system over to the Library?
questions: how are you handing the archival system over to the library
how do you mentor engineers
how do you train someone to take over a system
what's your approach to handoffs
cards.answer: I designed the engagement so the Library owns the result rather than depending on AITS. The incoming engineer's first professional project is a task ladder: it starts with environment setup and climbs to owning pipeline stages outright, with real deliverables rather than support work. I also gave her the manifest schema to review and sign off, with an explicit invitation to overturn my calls. If she's going to own it, she should get a real say in how it's built.

cards.title: How did you design the archival pipeline so someone else can own it?
questions: how did you design the archival pipeline so someone else can own it
why single-writer ownership
how do you make a pipeline maintainable
what's the manifest schema
cards.answer: I wrote an eight-stage pipeline design and a 116-column manifest schema that every stage reads and writes. Every field has exactly one owner: no stage writes a column another stage owns. That one rule is what makes each part independently testable, re-runnable and replaceable by an engineer other than me. If a stage breaks, you can fix and re-run just that stage without wondering what else it touched.

cards.title: What is the RIMS archival pipeline?
questions: what is the rims archival pipeline
tell me about your archival pipeline
what are you working on now at the university
what is rims
cards.answer: It's the production build that brings three of my archival AI proofs of concept, for email, images and mixed-format legacy files, together into one operational pipeline for the University Library and AITS Information Governance. I'm the technical lead and architect, and it started in August 2026. The work came by request: the University Archivist asked me to build the system, hand it off to the Library, and train her newly hired engineer toward owning it fully while I do. The stack is Python, Siegfried, ExifTool, FAISS, vLLM, LLaVA, Presidio, the Box API and Linux, and I'm also scoping the infrastructure to process the Archives at full corpus scale.

cards.title: How did you discover the archive throughput problem?
questions: how did you discover the archive throughput problem
why did you evaluate vllm
how do you find performance bottlenecks
cards.answer: Summarization was running at 34.78 seconds per record one at a time. That works out to roughly 966 hours for 100,000 records, and I traced it to the model being reloaded on every call. That led to a controlled serving-stack evaluation, which showed the real constraint was request serialization, not the hardware. Moving the backend to vLLM gave a 6.22x gain on the same hardware and cut full-corpus image processing from 22 hours to 3.7.

cards.title: What was wrong with the workforce report's likelihood column?
questions: what was wrong with the workforce report's likelihood column
have you ever found a statistical error in production
what is calibration and why does it matter
cards.answer: During stakeholder review I found that a column shown to leadership as a likelihood had never been calibrated against what actually happened, and readers were taking it literally. I replaced it with observed-rate bands, with cut points frozen out-of-time and validated by leave-one-year-out testing, and I wrote the stakeholder communication explaining the change. A number leadership reads as a probability has to behave like one.

cards.title: How did you make sure the workforce system can't be lost again?
questions: how did you make sure the workforce system can't be lost again
how do you document systems
how do you make pipelines resilient
cards.answer: I rebuilt it in Python with the specification frozen as a machine-checkable output contract, 4 files, 21 sheets and 436 columns, checked automatically on every run. I also built the point-in-time training panel the original never had. It runs quarterly on the institutional Linux server, is wired into cross-pipeline job monitoring, and is under version control, so it can't disappear with a server decommission again. I wrote a plain-language guide for leadership and a 33-page technical reference, and led the technical review with stakeholder leadership. Its outputs are summarized for executive leadership, including the President's office and CIO level.

cards.answer: The monitor is a modular Python application with one file per concern. log_reader.py loads and concatenates the pipeline Parquet logs into a single DataFrame. alert_rules.py classifies failures by status and age. time_windows.py holds the silence detection and the reusable last_n_hours and last_n_days filters. emailer.py builds and sends the alert mail. config.py holds the settings, including the list of extra log paths, and main.py runs the whole check. cards.answer: An unreadable log is treated as a failure, not skipped. If a pipeline's Parquet log is broken, corrupt or unreadable, the monitor writes a synthetic LOG_READ_FAILED record for it, so the problem shows up as an alert instead of the pipeline silently dropping out of view. It is tiered with real failures: LOG_READ_FAILED within the last 24 hours is CRITICAL, like a FAILED stage. The reasoning is simple. A monitor that quietly ignores logs it can't read would go blind exactly when the logging layer breaks, and the file path stored on each row helps me diagnose corruption or permission problems.

links.label: Email archiving case study: Data Pipeline & Ingestion

cards.answer: I converted a legacy .pst email archive into 44,677 .eml files using readpst, preserving the original folder structure. I used Python’s os.walk and the email library to parse MIME content, extracting text and headers with a UTF-8 fallback. I exploded message threads on the "-----Original Message-----" delimiter, increasing the row count from 44,677 to 79,676. The result was a flat CSV of structured message data.

links.label: Email archiving case study: PII Detection & Anonymization

cards.answer: I built an email archiving pipeline using Microsoft's presidio-analyzer to detect and anonymize PII. I configured the AnalyzerEngine to identify five entity types (PERSON, PHONE_NUMBER, EMAIL_ADDRESS, DATE_TIME, and US_SSN) each stored in a dedicated column. I used a spaCy NER model to detect names, replacing them with numbered placeholders like <PERSON1> while keeping original values in an auditable mapping dictionary. I made DATE_TIME detection aggressive enough to catch terms like "yesterday." To prevent offset errors, I ran replacements in reverse character order.

links.label: Email archiving case study: Topic Modeling & Content Discovery

cards.answer: I ran topic modeling on email subject lines and LLM-generated summaries using LDA and Llama 3.2, finding keyword clusters and readable topic labels. For subject lines, I used CountVectorizer with max_df=0.9, min_df=2, and LDA with n_components=5, uncovering the Abbott Power Plant procurement as the dominant topic across about 79,676 subject lines. For summaries, I used n_components=10, revealing a "Sensitive Email Briefing" cluster of 418 emails and HR themes not visible in subject lines. Summary-based clusters were richer due to consistent wording and absence of junk terms. I passed the top 10 keywords per topic to Llama 3.2 for 5-word-or-fewer labels.

cards.answer: I built a semantic search engine that embeds LLaMA-generated summaries into FAISS HNSW indexes for fast approximate nearest-neighbor lookup. Each index is 384-dimensional and persisted to disk, loading in seconds without re-embedding. The CLI supports top-k and threshold search, and the system uses LLaVA to index photos by description. A parallel Haystack setup with FAISSDocumentStore and EmbeddingRetriever allows easier integration of extractive QA or hybrid BM25 retrieval. The search space is clean and normalized because it indexes summaries rather than raw text.

cards.answer: For Skyrule, I built OCR tools to digitize historical books but found that model confidence doesn't always mean accuracy. Vision models misread symbols and failed to correct themselves. I learned to keep raw text untouched and normalize spelling only at search time, after a language model altered meanings in old text. About 850 pages were briefly lost when empty-page flags triggered, but a recovery step restored them, teaching me to track page counts at every stage. Numeric tables were handled separately because OCR alone couldn’t be trusted on them.

cards.answer: I built a 26-field taxonomy for the NSF HERDS classification system, using a curated and deduplicated keyword list with eight reassignments adjudicated per keyword. cards.answer: I designed a controlled vLLM evaluation using 50 identical 4,500 to 4,972 Mistral-token bills across three models: Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3 AWQ, Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct AWQ, and Llama 3.1 8B Instruct AWQ. Each model ran at its quality-best chunk size, avoiding forced uniformity, what I call the Olympic swimmer principle. I measured TTFT, ITL p50/p99, decode and prefill throughput with 10-second GPU sampling and no safety alarms. Setup used vLLM 0.6.6, AWQ-Marlin, --max-model-len 8192, prefix caching, and a 5-call warmup. cards.answer: I built a rubric with three dimensions scored 0 to 2: Accuracy, Specificity and Completeness. Accuracy measures from wrong (0) to faithful to this chunk (2). The per-cell average is (Accuracy + Specificity + Completeness) / 3.

cards.answer: I assume leakage until I've ruled it out, especially when a number looks great. In bill prediction, procedural history leaks by construction: the actions that record a bill passing live in the same table as the actions that predict it. cards.answer: I treat chunk size as a measured parameter, measured on the real length distribution. On the legislative pipeline every 7B-class model degraded past roughly 2,000 tokens, which let me choose chunk size separately from the model. The vLLM sweep then showed what parse rates hid: larger chunks caused off-section drift, where the model answers confidently about a neighboring section of the bill. Llama 3.1 8B at 1,200 tokens stayed on-chunk and reached 92.5% parse-OK, while a 14B model given whole 5,000-token bills scored 45.0%, so more context made things worse. I also check boundary artifacts: a dip at 4,000 tokens turned out to be thin tail chunks. When a document must be summarized whole, I compress it semantically first, keeping the 250 most representative sentences rather than truncating the head.

cards.answer: I get reliable structured output by forcing a schema, counting parse status as its own quality signal and keeping code responsible for anything exact. Every chunk is marked OK, PARTIAL or EMPTY, so malformed output is counted rather than silently absorbed. On the archival images, one combined prompt returning JSON for all six fields was 1.61x faster than three calls and parsed 100% on five fields and 94% on the title. cards.answer: I built a generative Markov chain model to simulate probable career journeys from any starting role across N moves. It uses a career transition matrix built from parsed past_job_titles sequences as input. The simulate_career_path function walks transitions stochastically, while simulate_many_paths summarizes final-role distributions. The output is a probability distribution of career destinations from any starting job title. links.label: Research Proposal Processing Pipeline: The HERDS Taxonomy

cards.answer: I built the HERDS classifier to score all 26 research fields at once using a single matrix multiplication. Each proposal is embedded with the same SentenceTransformer used by KeyBERT, then multiplied against a pre-computed taxonomy-embedding matrix. This matrix covers all 26 HERDS fields, allowing classification in one operation rather than 26 separate queries. The taxonomy embeddings are built once and cached to disk.

links.label: UIC Student Enrollment Prediction: Data Preparation

cards.answer: I built four label variations for the UIC enrollment model to test different definitions of student continuation. Next Term labeled continuation as 1 if a student enrolled in the immediately following fall or spring term, with summer skips not penalized, graduation as 2, and dropout as 0. Next Year (Any Term) was more forgiving of gaps, checking for enrollment in any term within the following academic year. Next Fall Only isolated the strongest signal by looking only for fall term re-enrollment in the following year. Binary Success collapsed continuation and graduation into a single success label (1), with dropout as 0.

cards.answer: I built an OCR system for 170 historical books, spanning 22,700 pages printed from the 1480s to the 1850s. Pages had multi-column layouts, footnotes, tables, diagrams, woodcuts, and poor microfilm scans.

cards.answer: I evaluated vLLM models using three quality signals. The first signal is a structural validity check, parse-OK rate, across all 15 fields, fast and scalable but not sufficient. The second is a blind rubric scoring of 60 cells across three models' best configurations to confirm parse-OK ranked them correctly. cards.answer: I evaluated vLLM inference throughput across chunk sizes and found that Llama is the only model to clear 80% parse-OK at every size tested. cards.answer: I evaluated vLLM inference throughput and found that at chunk_size=4,000, each bill split into a full 4,000-token chunk and a short 500 to 900-token tail chunk. At chunk_size=5,000, the same bills became single chunks and Mistral's parse-OK recovered to exactly 72.0%, matching its chunk_size=3,000 result. cards.answer: In experiment 3, I designed a scoring system using Claude Opus 4.8 to evaluate 60 cells (3 profiles, 20 chunks, and 3 dimensions) on a 0 to 2 rubric for Accuracy, Specificity, and Completeness. cards.answer: I evaluated how context-window size affects extraction fidelity in vLLM configurations. The 3,000-token Mistral config often pulled in adjacent bill sections and lost the chunk’s headline. The 1,200-token Llama config stayed on-chunk most reliably. cards.answer: I evaluated vLLM inference quality using a chunk-fidelity scoring approach, measuring whether each model correctly extracted a specific chunk. At Chunk 8, Mistral returned a highly specific but off-topic answer from the same bill, scoring Accuracy:1 under chunk-fidelity. cards.answer: I measured Mistral's root cause as KV cache head-of-line blocking, with preemption at concurrency eight or higher due to L4's 22.5 GB VRAM limits. I proposed three optimization paths: reducing chunk size to 2,000 tokens to ease cache pressure and improve quality, increasing vLLM swap space from 4 GB to 16+ GB, and adjusting chunking strategy to match real-world data like short bills.

cards.answer: I evaluated Qwen 7B’s failure modes and two paths. I read None-emission, where all 11 fields return None, as a prompt compliance issue, not a model capability one. Path 1 is to add explicit field-completion requirements, return 'not mentioned' rather than null, and two-shot examples, then rerun Exp 3.5 Pair 2 and measure whether None-emission drops below 5%. Path 2 is chunk_size=2,000 as the operating point, since it scored 1.93 quality versus 1.57 at chunk_size=3,000. Qwen’s ITL p99 of 118ms versus Llama’s 49ms is likely caused by its tokenizer; capping max_tokens at 768 may stabilize ITL.

cards.answer: I evaluated Qwen 14B's output constraints and found that at 5,000 input tokens, the model lacked headroom to complete 11-field JSON responses, with 54% partial parses and 1.2 missing fields on average. Path 1: increase max_tokens to 2,048, which gives about 2x output headroom at roughly 40 to 60% slower per call; Path 2: reduce chunk_size to 2,000, which leaves about 3,000 tokens of output headroom. cards.answer: During the extended sweep, I spotted silent failures where launches exited with code 0 but produced incomplete results. cards.answer: I designed the vLLM evaluation to make a production decision, not to run a benchmark, because choosing the wrong model could become a liability as more states are added. cards.answer: The article covers selecting a production LLM for the Illinois Legislation Pipeline, which extracts structured intelligence across 15 fields from state bills. The evaluation ran 126 cells across six experiments over two weeks, with a blind qualitative review of 60 cells and a production SLO projection. The constraint was a single NVIDIA L4 GPU with 22.5 GB VRAM, open weight models only, running locally under vLLM. The candidates were Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3 AWQ, Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct AWQ and Llama 3.1 8B Instruct AWQ. A prior March 2026 evaluation used Ollama and Llama 3.2 3B; the rerun added concurrency measurement and parameter parity.

cards.answer: The article shows the Illinois corpus has a median bill length of 1,051 tokens, 75% under 3,500 tokens, and a tail to 1 million tokens. Mistral's parse-OK dropped from 72% to 59.8% at chunk size 4,000 because sample bills split into a 500 to 900 token tail chunk and recovered to 72.0% at 5,000. The SLO was about 75,000 bills per week at 50-state scale in an 18-hour window and the gap on one L4 was 3.16x steady state and 6.57x peak burst. Three L4s in parallel or one A100-class GPU would close the steady-state gap. The four practices are to test on your actual data, measure quality separately from structure, test at production concurrency, and measure the tail not the mean.

links.label: The Metrics That Lied to Us: article

cards.answer: I write that Mistral’s p99 latency jumps fivefold from concurrency 1 to 24, from 15 seconds to 74 seconds, with a sharp increase between c=4 and c=8. The cause is KV cache head-of-line blocking: Mistral’s 3,000 token prompts require large KV cache allocations, and at higher concurrency, the GPU VRAM can’t hold all in-flight KV states, leading to preemption and recomputation. At concurrency 24, Mistral’s p99 latency was 74 seconds compared to 39 seconds for Llama and 19 seconds for Qwen. This 74 second p99 meant roughly 1% of bill extractions blocked the processing queue for over a minute, and Mistral was eliminated because its chunk-size configuration was incompatible with the pipeline’s concurrency requirements.

cards.answer: Starting on-prem with a fully contained LLM was a choice I still stand by. On-prem, we weren’t constrained by API limits or cloud permissions, and we weren’t watching costs every batch. That let us run large-scale experiments freely, iterate on prompts and chunking strategies, and process massive volumes of text without artificial ceilings. When every iteration has a price tag, you end up optimizing for cost instead of learning. By the time we moved to cloud, the system was already shaped, so the cloud became a scaling layer, not a guessing layer. cards.answer: Agent territory: ambiguous decisions, logical reasoning, evolving inputs. The example I use is scraping trending topics in news. You can't hard-code what's trending, it changes constantly, and the model has to look at generalities and pick top themes. That's genuine agent work. Workflow automation: static process, consistent algorithm, consistent input and output. Same shape data coming in, same shape data going out. Don't use an agent for that. RPA: the simplest stuff, standard ETL, standard in and standard out. Old-school data science methods handle this perfectly. You don't need an AI agent. Rule of thumb: if the task requires the system to interpret something that isn't clearly defined, it's an agent. If it doesn't, it isn't, and forcing AI into it just adds complexity and cost.

cards.answer: Yes. I don't think agents are just an evolution of automation and APIs with better UX. They're a real shift in how work gets done. The part that's fundamentally different is ambiguity. Traditional pipelines follow deterministic logic, rule-based, conditional, predictable in. Agents operate where the decision isn't something you can hard-code. Where the model has to make a judgment call on fuzzy inputs. That's both the power and the risk. You're handing off the ambiguity to the AI, and whatever it decides is what happens next. If you think your role is safe, it probably isn't. Within the next 6 to 12 months, tasks, not whole jobs, but tasks, are going to start getting stripped out of roles at an accelerating pace. Whether that's a problem depends on your job. If it's mostly repetitive, yeah, be concerned. If it involves real decision-making, stakeholder work, strategy, and business impact, you're likely fine, but your job will evolve.

cards.answer: There has to be a way to anchor outputs back to truth. AI systems drift. The more they build on prior outputs, the worse it gets. So you need a base truth layer, validated data, known-good outputs, plus a way to detect drift and cross-check results. Some tolerance for variation is fine. Unlimited deviation isn't. My concrete example: in my legislation work, I have the Llama model generating category labels (new-school) and I also have an old-school clustering model generating categories from keywords (old-school). Both produce taxonomies. If one says Higher Education and the other says K-12 for the same bill, that's a flag. I can isolate the mismatches, inspect them, and figure out whether the model drifted or the data is weird. Hybrid validation like that is essential.

cards.answer: Everyone says 'AI augments humans' but most of the time that's vague or not really true. Both are happening simultaneously. The difference is what kind of work and how much oversight exists. Real augmentation: AI helps you move faster, you still own the outcome. You review, validate, correct, make the final call. Where humans must stay in control right now: hiring, firing, legal outcomes, financial decisions, anything that directly affects someone's life. Those need multiple layers of review: the person who built the system approves how it works, stakeholders own the decisions, and someone audits continuously. Without that, it's not augmentation, it's uncontrolled automation in a trench coat.

cards.answer: When I was extracting 10+ structured features from legislation text, I originally thought asking each question separately would make parsing cleaner and more predictable. Turns out that's wrong. Bundling the questions in the same prompt gave better results because the model uses its earlier answers as context for later ones. If it already established 'this impacts higher education' and 'this affects students,' then when I later ask 'does this impact the university,' it answers yes coherently, and when I ask 'rate the impact as slight/moderate/very impactful,' it uses everything it just figured out. Context builds within the prompt. Isolating tasks too much loses coherence and reasoning continuity. Prompt engineering isn't just asking questions, it's designing the context the model reasons inside.

Cloud-based closed models are also problematic for use cases where I need guarantees about what's happening with the data. Anything involving private or sensitive data that shouldn't be leaving a controlled environment. If it's PII, legislation with exposure risk, or anything high-stakes and private, I'd containerize the model on an on-prem server and wouldn't involve third-party services. The trade-off is less raw model power, but for a lot of tasks that's fine.

cards.title: The outlier bills that broke my pipeline

100000 token bills

a time preprocessing saved your pipeline
cards.answer: In my legislation work, some bills were massive outliers, over 100,000 tokens, roughly 100x the size of a normal bill. Only about 5% of the data, but they added enormous noise. They were amendment-heavy bills, the same content updated over and over with every small change. Most of it added no context. What actually mattered was the latest changes, maybe the last thousand tokens. If you feed those directly into an AI system without preprocessing, it chunks them inefficiently, wastes compute, takes hours to process the worst-quality subset, and pollutes everything downstream. The fix wasn't an AI fix. It was a preprocessing fix. Detect the outliers, summarize them as 'amendment type, last changes attached,' and move on. Good data preprocessing should never be wasted AI logic.

People are jumping over fundamentals. Data is messy, inconsistent, poorly structured, and everyone's trying to skip the preprocessing and cleaning. Cool demos, consistent production failure. We need 2 to 3 years for companies that start now, maybe 5 for the stragglers. Want AI to do the magical stuff? Start with your data today.

Human-created art. Live music in a hot crowded venue with a sweaty microphone. Handmade pottery. Pottery with brushstrokes and imperfections. Food cooked and served by a person. In-person experiences. Not because AI can't replicate them, but because people will choose to value the human version. We've spent decades optimizing efficiency, scale, and output at the cost of connection, creativity, and experience. This might be the correction. And if nobody values that? Then yeah, we're doomed. cards.answer: People box ROI into time saved, cost reduced, revenue generated. That's incomplete. One of AI's most underrated capabilities is extracting insight that was previously inaccessible. What are the things you don't know? What are you losing because you didn't know them? That's the cost of not knowing, and it's where AI really earns its place. My legislation work is the clearest example. Being aware of what's being proposed before it passes lets you prevent losses and find opportunities. In HR, detecting where roles are shrinking or growing ahead of time is strategic intelligence. Not time. Not cost. Better decisions, better strategy, better plans.

cards.title: The model needs to know what the data means
questions: how do you evaluate an llm or a rag system? what metrics do you trust?
does an llm need a data dictionary
why does metadata matter for ai
data cookbook
how do you give a model schema context
confident garbage
how does a model understand my tables
help a model understand our database tables
cards.answer: Even if the data is technically correct, if the model doesn't understand what the fields represent, it'll produce confident garbage. Poorly named columns, encoded values with no explanation, missing metadata, no documentation, all of it breaks the system quietly. You need a context layer: a data dictionary or 'data cookbook,' metadata descriptions, schema explanations embedded into prompts. It needs to know what each field represents, how fields relate, and what the data is actually capturing. Without that you're asking it to interpret something it doesn't understand, and it'll happily make something up.

cards.answer: In the AI era, things look convincingly right even when they're wrong. Code generation is fast. Analysis is fast. But so much of it is wrong in subtle ways. The real job now is validation, combing through line by line, column by column, asking where the data came from, whether it makes sense. If I'm getting 100% accuracy on a model, something is wrong. If everything is falling into place too easily, something is wrong. The job of a data scientist now is to slow it down.

cards.answer: I started in service work in Austin, Texas, at a place called Casino El Camino, a dive bar on Sixth Street. After moving back to San Diego, I spent a year all in on art with group shows at La Bodega Gallery, Thumbprint Gallery and Mike Hess Brewing but realized it wouldn't pay the bills. I worked at Starbucks while going to MiraCosta College, a community college, taking rigorous math to prepare for engineering. I transferred to UC San Diego for nanoengineering but switched to cognitive science because it offered a breadth that included data science, coding, neuroscience, psychology, child development, the brain, even art. I still love it. I have real interest in a PhD in cognitive science at UC San Diego but I am so productive teaching myself and building things that I am not sure school is in my best interest unless it meant hands-on work in a research lab.
